advisories.summary: Pillow: Heap buffer overflow saving TIFF with libtiff when tags override image size
advisories.description:
```
============================================================================
ANT-2026-CS7N494P  [high]  CWE-787  memory-safety
Heap buffer overflow saving TIFF with libtiff when tags override image size
Location: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1035  in ImagingLibTiffEncode()
Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6
============================================================================
```

When Pillow saves an image as a compressed TIFF, size information taken from the image's metadata can make the encoder read past the end of a heap buffer. Someone who uploads an image can use this to get the server process's memory, including pointers, copied into the saved file, or to crash the process. When the metadata also enables TIFF "Predictor=2" compression, the encoder writes past the buffer instead, corrupting the heap and aborting the process. This affects applications that write TIFF through libtiff (any `compression=` other than raw) and either carry the source metadata across with `exif=im.getexif()` / `tiffinfo=`, or simply re-save a crafted palette TIFF with `Image.open(f).save(out, "TIFF")`, which inherits its compression and predictor from the upload.

In `TiffImagePlugin._save`'s libtiff branch, only `BitsPerSample` is pinned to the real image when the tag list for the encoder is built (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1955`). `ImageWidth`, `ImageLength` and `PlanarConfiguration` are set from `im.size` but are then overwritten by the `exif=`/`tiffinfo=` merge loop at `:1768-1772`. `SamplesPerPixel` is never set for single-band modes, so a value from the caller's tags or from the source TIFF's own IFD reaches `TIFFSetField`. `ImagingLibTiffEncode` then passes a row buffer sized from the actual image (`src/encode.c:291`) to `TIFFWriteScanline` (`src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1035`) with no check against `TIFFScanlineSize()`, and libtiff consumes a full scanline of the tag-described width from it.

The attached reproducer demonstrates the read case. A 64x4 greyscale JPEG whose EXIF says `SamplesPerPixel=3, Photometric=RGB` is converted into a valid RGB TIFF in which 128 bytes of each row are live heap, including pointers that change from run to run. The same JPEG with EXIF `ImageWidth=2**27` kills the process with SIGSEGV. For the write case, the values written are byte-wise differences of existing heap contents rather than attacker-chosen data, and nothing beyond the observed glibc abort is shown. The `tiffinfo=` route dates back to Pillow 2.3.0 (`dbf47837ce99`), and the `exif=` route to 8.4.0 (`c0f619384cbc`).

## Details

When an image is saved as TIFF through the libtiff encoder (any `compression=` other than raw, or `TiffImagePlugin.WRITE_LIBTIFF`), libtiff sizes its scanline from the `ImageWidth` / `SamplesPerPixel` / `BitsPerSample` / `PlanarConfiguration` tags it was handed, Pillow sizes the encoder row buffer from the real image, and nothing compares the two. In `TiffImagePlugin._save`'s libtiff branch only `BitsPerSample` is pinned in the attribute dict given to the encoder (`atts`, `src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1955-1982`); the other geometry tags can come from caller- or attacker-supplied data:

- `ImageWidth` (256), `ImageLength` (257) and `PlanarConfiguration` (284) are set from `im.size` *before* the `tiffinfo=` / `exif=` merge loop at `:1768-1772`, so they are overwritten by it — by the EXIF of an uploaded JPEG, or by stale geometry in `im.getexif()` / `im.tag_v2` of a TIFF that Pillow auto-transposed on load (Orientation tag) or that the application `thumbnail()`ed.
- `SamplesPerPixel` (277) is only put in the IFD for multi-band modes (`:1847-1850`), so for single-band images (`L`, `P`, `I;16`, `1`, …) a value from `exif=` / `tiffinfo=`, or from the *source TIFF's own IFD* via `supplied_tags` (`im.tag_v2`, `:1782`), is forwarded to libtiff. A palette TIFF with `SamplesPerPixel=2, BitsPerSample=(8,8), ExtraSamples=(0,)` opens as mode `P` (rawmode `PX`, extra sample dropped), and a bare `im.save(out, "TIFF")` — no save arguments; `compression` and `Predictor` are inherited from the source — already makes libtiff process `2*width` bytes per row from a `width`-byte buffer.

`ImagingLibTiffEncode` then hands the image-sized row buffer to `TIFFWriteScanline`, and libtiff reads one scanline of the *tag-described* geometry out of a buffer holding one row of the *actual* image. With `Predictor = 2` (also forwarded from `tiffinfo=` / `im.tag_v2`) libtiff's horizontal differencing first rewrites the whole scanline **in place**, so the over-read becomes an out-of-bounds heap **write** on every row.

The tags do not have to be supplied deliberately by the application: `im.getexif()` of an uploaded JPEG returns whatever IFD0 tags the file carries, and the common metadata-preserving conversion

```python
im = Image.open(uploaded_jpeg)                                   # 64x4, mode "L"
im.save(out, "TIFF", exif=im.getexif(), compression="tiff_lzw")
```

behaves as follows on the stock build at this commit:

- EXIF IFD0 `{277: 3, 262: 2}` (SamplesPerPixel=3, Photometric=RGB): the save succeeds and `out` is a 64x4 **RGB** TIFF. Re-opening it, the first 64 bytes of every 192-byte row are the image (0x11 fill); the remaining 128 bytes are heap that followed the 64-byte row buffer — e.g. `... 807a97e6527f0000 ... f03632e5527f0000 40832ee5527f0000` (x86-64 heap pointers), different on every run.
- EXIF IFD0 `{256: 1<<27}` (ImageWidth=2^27): the process dies with SIGSEGV; gdb shows `TIFFWriteScanline (libtiff.so.6) ← ImagingLibTiffEncode (src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1035) ← _encode (src/encode.c:139)`.
- valgrind on the first case: `Invalid read of size 1 … TIFFWriteScanline … by ImagingLibTiffEncode … Address is 0 bytes after a block of size 64 alloc'd at calloc by _setimage`.
- Control: the same JPEG with an EXIF holding only `Software` produces a 64x4 `L` TIFF whose 256 pixel bytes are all 0x11.

The write variant needs nothing more than a well-formed 222-byte TIFF and the `exif=im.getexif()` idiom the project's own tests use (`Tests/test_file_tiff.py::test_exif`, `test_modify_exif`); the interpreter dies with glibc's `free(): invalid next size (fast)` (SIGABRT):

```python
from PIL import Image; import io
b = io.BytesIO()
Image.new("RGB", (64, 4)).save(b, "TIFF", compression="tiff_lzw", tiffinfo={274: 6, 317: 2})  # Orientation=6, Predictor=2
im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(b.getvalue())); im.load()   # auto-transposed to 4x64; tag_v2/getexif() still say 64x4
im.save(io.BytesIO(), "TIFF", exif=im.getexif())       # or tiffinfo=im.tag_v2
```

Here libtiff processes 192-byte rows (64 px × 3 samples) from the 12-byte buffer `_setimage` allocated for a 4-pixel RGB row, and `PredictorEncodeRow` rewrites the 180 heap bytes that follow it on each of 64 rows; valgrind on a `-g` build reports `Invalid write of size 1 … TIFFWriteScanline … by ImagingLibTiffEncode (TiffDecode.c:1035) … Address is 0 bytes after a block of size 12 alloc'd … by _setimage (encode.c:293)`. `im.thumbnail((8, 8))` before the save instead of the Orientation tag reaches the same state, as does the purely programmatic `Image.new("RGB", (128, 32)).save(fp, "TIFF", compression="tiff_lzw", tiffinfo={256: 1024, 257: 128, 317: 2})` (SIGSEGV). For the source-IFD `SamplesPerPixel` route, a crafted <2 KB palette `PX` TIFF with `Compression = LZW, Predictor = 2` kills the stock build on a bare `Image.open(f).save(out, "TIFF")`; with a predictor-less codec the same re-save returns normally with `width` bytes of heap per row encoded into the output.

### Walk-through

`_save` seeds the output IFD from the image and then copies the caller's tags over it:

```python
# src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py
1746    libtiff = WRITE_LIBTIFF or compression != "raw"
1749    ifd[PLANAR_CONFIGURATION] = 1
1751    ifd[IMAGEWIDTH] = im.size[0]
1752    ifd[IMAGELENGTH] = im.size[1]
        …
1757    elif "exif" in encoderinfo:
1758        info = encoderinfo["exif"]          # Image.Exif, or bytes → Exif
        …
1768    for key in info:
            …
1772            ifd[key] = info.get(key)            # 256/257/277/262/284/317 … overwrite the above
```

The geometry is only partially re-asserted afterwards: `BITSPERSAMPLE` is always set, but `SAMPLESPERPIXEL` only for multi-band modes and `IMAGEWIDTH`/`IMAGELENGTH` never:

```python
1847    if bits != (1,):
1848        ifd[BITSPERSAMPLE] = bits
1849        if len(bits) != 1:
1850            ifd[SAMPLESPERPIXEL] = len(bits)    # not reached for L, P, I, F, I;16 …
1856    if PHOTOMETRIC_INTERPRETATION not in ifd:   # supplied value kept
```

In the libtiff branch every IFD entry that is not block-listed — and, after the IFD, every entry of `supplied_tags` (the source file's `im.tag_v2`) not already present — becomes a `TIFFSetField` argument. The only tag pinned to the image's real value is `BITSPERSAMPLE`:

```python
1955        atts: dict[int, Any] = {BITSPERSAMPLE: bits[0]}
1959        for tag, value in itertools.chain(ifd.items(), supplied_tags.items()):
            …
1976            if tag not in atts and tag not in blocklist:
                    …   atts[tag] = value
2002        encoder = Image._getencoder(im.mode, "libtiff", a, encoderconfig)
2003        encoder.setimage(im.im, (0, 0, *im.size))
```

For the SamplesPerPixel=3 example the tag list passed to the encoder is `[(256, 64), (257, 4), (258, 8), (259, 5), (262, 2), (277, 3), (278, 4), (284, 1)]`; for the ImageWidth example it is `[(256, 134217728), (257, 4), (258, 8), …]`. 256 and 277 are in `core_tags` (`src/encode.c:694`), so `PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew` forwards them straight to `TIFFSetField`. For a single-band image `SAMPLESPERPIXEL` is absent from `ifd`, so the loop takes tag 277 from `supplied_tags` — the source TIFF's IFD — when one is present; the `PLANAR_CONFIGURATION == 2` adjustment at `:1783-1788` already compensates for this for separate-planes sources, the contiguous `PX` layout is the remaining case.

`encoder.setimage` sizes the packer's row buffer from the real image — 64 bytes for a 64-pixel `L` row:

```c
/* src/encode.c, _setimage */
287    if (state->bits > 0) {
291        state->bytes = (state->bits * state->xsize + 7) / 8;
293        state->buffer = (UINT8 *)calloc(1, state->bytes);
```

and `ImagingLibTiffEncode` packs one image row into it and gives the pointer to libtiff with no length:

```c
/* src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c */
1027        while (state->y < state->ysize) {
1028            state->shuffle(state->buffer, (UINT8 *)im->image[state->y + state->yoff] + …, state->xsize);
1035            if (TIFFWriteScanline(tiff, (tdata_t)(state->buffer), (uint32_t)state->y, 0) == -1) {
```

`TIFFWriteScanline` consumes `TIFFScanlineSize()` bytes, i.e. `ImageWidth * SamplesPerPixel * BitsPerSample / 8` as set through the tags. Nothing between `_save` and line 1035 compares that with `state->bytes`. With SamplesPerPixel=3 libtiff reads 192 bytes from the 64-byte block and LZW-encodes the trailing 128 heap bytes into the strip; with ImageWidth=2^27 it reads 128 MiB starting at the 64-byte block and faults. With `Predictor = 2`, libtiff's `PredictorEncodeRow` first runs horizontal differencing in place over the whole scanline (`bp[i] -= bp[i-stride]`), i.e. it rewrites the heap bytes that follow the block before encoding them; libtiff grows `ImageLength` as rows beyond the declared count are written, so every row of the real image goes through. A `PlanarConfiguration = 2` carried over from a planar source reaches libtiff by the same route; there libtiff's scanline (one sample plane) is shorter than Pillow's row, so the result is an undecodable file rather than an out-of-bounds access.

The non-libtiff path (`compression` absent/raw) is not affected: it goes through `ImagingRawEncode`, which treats the IFD-derived stride as padding and either zero-fills or fails with `IMAGING_CODEC_CONFIG` (`src/libImaging/RawEncode.c:34-37,57-59`). Overriding `IMAGEWIDTH`/`IMAGELENGTH` through `tiffinfo` on that path is an intended feature (`Tests/test_file_tiff.py::test_tiff_chunks`).

The `exif=` route was introduced in `c0f619384cbc` ("Added "exif" keyword argument to save Image.Exif instance", 2021-07-04), first released in 8.4.0. The same override through `tiffinfo=` is older: it dates back to `dbf47837ce99` ("Add arbitrary tags to tiff images using an ImageFileDirectory", 2013-10-02, first in 2.3.0). The stale-geometry-from-the-file-itself form dates from `1b70a4c6b515` ("Use TIFF orientation", 2019-09-13, first in 6.2.0), which added the transpose on load.

## Impact

Affected are applications that write TIFF output from user-supplied images through libtiff. Through the source-IFD `SamplesPerPixel` route nothing more is needed than `Image.open(f).save(out, "TIFF")` (format normalisation) on a crafted palette TIFF: `Compression`, `SamplesPerPixel` and `Predictor` are all inherited from the upload, so the uploader chooses between heap corruption / worker abort (`Predictor = 2`) and a normally-returning save whose output carries `width` bytes of the worker's heap per row. The `exif=` / `tiffinfo=` routes cover applications that convert to compressed TIFF while carrying the metadata across — `im.save(..., "TIFF", compression="tiff_lzw"|"tiff_adobe_deflate"|"packbits"|"jpeg"|…, exif=im.getexif())`, `exif=im.info["exif"]`, or `tiffinfo=` built from the source file's tags. Neither option is a default, but both are ordinary settings for archival/print/scan pipelines and the idiom used in Pillow's own tests. The uploader then chooses the outcome through a few EXIF shorts: a small `SamplesPerPixel` (with a matching `Photometric` so the result is a valid RGB/CMYK TIFF) returns `(spp-1) × width` bytes of process heap per image row inside the produced file — for a 4000-pixel-wide upload that is 8 KB of heap per row, megabytes per file, readable with any TIFF decoder and containing allocator metadata, pointers (ASLR defeat) and whatever other requests left in freed memory; a large `ImageWidth` kills the worker with SIGSEGV; `ImageWidth`/`ImageLength` larger than the (transposed or thumbnailed) image together with `Predictor = 2` writes `(declared_width − real_width) × bytes_per_pixel` bytes past a small fresh `calloc` block on every row — the values written are byte-wise differences of the existing heap contents, so the attacker controls extent and repetition but not directly the data; the observed result is heap corruption and abort of the whole worker, exploitation beyond that is not demonstrated. Because `ImageWidth`/`ImageLength` are routinely present in IFD0 of camera and scanner output, a benign photo that is resized before such a save also over-reads (its EXIF still describes the original width), so the crash variant can occur without an attacker.

## Reproducing

`repro` is a single Python script that uses the installed Pillow and only its public API; no rebuild is needed. It runs in well under a second.

It builds the attacker's input in memory: a 64x4 JPEG in mode `L` with every pixel set to 0x11, plus a chosen set of EXIF IFD0 tags. It then runs the metadata-preserving conversion an application would do:

```python
im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(jpeg))
im.save(out, "TIFF", exif=im.getexif(), compression="tiff_lzw")
```

Finally it re-opens the TIFF that comes out. There are three cases:

- **control**: the EXIF holds only `Software`. The output is a 64x4 `L` TIFF whose 256 bytes are all 0x11. The verdict can only be `BUG` if this holds.
- **leak**: the EXIF holds `SamplesPerPixel=3, PhotometricInterpretation=RGB`. libtiff now treats each scanline as 192 bytes, but the row buffer only holds 64 bytes. The save still succeeds and the output is a 64x4 **`RGB`** TIFF. In each 192-byte row, the first 64 bytes are the image (0x11). The other 128 bytes are whatever sat in the heap after the 64-byte row buffer.
  - The script hex-dumps row 0's extra bytes. They include x86-64 pointers such as `…e06c297e677f0000`, which change from run to run because of ASLR.
  - It also counts the extra bytes that are neither 0x11 nor 0x00, since those could not have come from the image or from zero padding. On the stock build this is a few hundred of the 512 bytes (200–310 in our runs).
- **crash**: the EXIF holds `ImageWidth=2**27`. The script re-runs itself as a child process (`repro crash`) with core dumps disabled. libtiff tries to read 128 MiB out of the 64-byte buffer, and the child dies with SIGSEGV (exit code -11).

Expected output on the stock build (the heap bytes and the count vary):

```
control: L (64, 4), all bytes 0x11: True
leak:    RGB (64, 4)
         first 64 bytes of each row are the image (0x11): True
         row 0, bytes 64..192 (past the row buffer):
           0000000000000000310000000000000090e5b50669550000e06c297e677f0000
           0000000001007900007b8804d80c0d8830000000000000001007000000000000
           0100000000000000801a897e677f0000240300000000000030444a7d677f0000
           4095487d677f0000885f897e677f000003000001010000000000000000000000
         220 of 512 bytes past the row buffers are neither 0x11 nor 0x00
crash:   child exit code -11 (SIGSEGV)
BUG
```

The last line is `BUG` if the control is clean and the leak case produced foreign bytes, the crash case died with SIGSEGV/SIGBUS, or both. Otherwise it is `OK`.

With either attached patch applied and rebuilt, the script prints:

```
control: L (64, 4), all bytes 0x11: True
leak:    output is not a readable image (no over-read)
crash:   child exit code 0 (no signal)
OK
```

In the leak case, the fixed build writes the image's real single sample per pixel but keeps the supplied `Photometric=RGB`. Pillow will not open a TIFF like that.

The out-of-bounds write variant is the three-line `Orientation=6, Predictor=2` snippet in Details (SIGABRT, `free(): invalid next size (fast)` on the stock build); for a file:line stack run it under valgrind on a `-g` build of the extensions.

## Suggested fix

Two alternative patches are attached. Patch 2 is the Python-only subset of patch 1; patch 1 also hardens the C encoder.

**Attached patch 1** (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py`, `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`) does two independent things:

1. `src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1955` — the libtiff branch already pre-seeds `atts` with `BITSPERSAMPLE` so that no supplied tag can replace it. The patch extends that to the other tags that determine libtiff's scanline size, taken from the image being saved:

```diff
-        atts: dict[int, Any] = {BITSPERSAMPLE: bits[0]}
+        atts: dict[int, Any] = {
+            BITSPERSAMPLE: bits[0],
+            SAMPLESPERPIXEL: len(bits),
+            IMAGEWIDTH: im.size[0],
+            IMAGELENGTH: im.size[1],
+            PLANAR_CONFIGURATION: 1,
+        }
```

   Doing it here rather than in the IFD built at 1749–1772 leaves the raw-writer behaviour exercised by `test_tiff_chunks` untouched, and because the merge loop visits `ifd` and `supplied_tags` only for tags not already in `atts`, it closes the `exif=`, `tiffinfo=` and source-IFD (`im.tag_v2`) routes alike. A supplied `PHOTOMETRIC_INTERPRETATION` still reaches the file (so EXIF `{277:3, 262:2}` now yields a 1-sample "RGB" TIFF that Pillow refuses to open); whether to force it to the mode's value is a format decision that no longer affects memory safety. For the re-saved `PX` palette case it may also be worth dropping the source's `EXTRASAMPLES` from `supplied_tags` (meaningless once the extra channel was discarded on load), as is already done for the planar case at `:1783-1788`, so the output is a self-consistent 1-sample palette file.

2. `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`, `ImagingLibTiffEncode` — before the scanline loop, it refuses any configuration in which libtiff would read more than the packer produced, so the encoder stays safe regardless of where tags come from:

```c
        if (TIFFScanlineSize64(tiff) > (uint64_t)state->bytes) {
            state->errcode = IMAGING_CODEC_CONFIG;
            ImagingLibTiffEncodeCleanup(state);
            clientstate->tiff = NULL;
            if (!clientstate->fp) {
                free(clientstate->data);
            }
            return -1;
        }
```

   The same cleanup is applied to the existing `TIFFWriteScanline` error path. For in-memory output, that path currently frees `clientstate->data` but leaves `clientstate->tiff` set, so the later `ImagingLibTiffEncodeCleanup` → `TIFFClose` → `TIFFFlush` writes into the freed buffer. Both error paths now close the TIFF before the data is freed. The `TIFFFlush` failure branch further down (`src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1056`) has the same pattern and is left as it is.

**Attached patch 2** (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py` only) is step 1 above without the C changes, for maintainers who prefer not to touch the encoder. It closes every public-API route (`exif=`, `tiffinfo=`, a resized or transposed image's carried-over EXIF/`tag_v2`) by which these tags reach `TIFFSetField`. `ImagingLibTiffEncode` still trusts its tag list, though, and the error-path use-after-free described above stays as it is.

Both patches add `Tests/test_file_libtiff.py::test_geometry_tags`, parametrised over oversized `IMAGEWIDTH`/`IMAGELENGTH`, `SAMPLESPERPIXEL=3` and `PLANAR_CONFIGURATION=2`. With either patch applied to a clean checkout and rebuilt, `repro` prints `OK`, the `Predictor = 2` snippet in Details saves a 4×64 image normally, and the existing TIFF test suites still pass.

```python
    image_part = b"".join(pixels[y * row : y * row + W] for y in range(H))
    beyond = b"".join(pixels[y * row + W : (y + 1) * row] for y in range(H))
    # Bytes that are neither the image's grey nor zero padding can only be heap contents.
    foreign = sum(b not in (GREY, 0) for b in beyond)
    print(f"leak:    {tiff.mode} {tiff.size}")
    print(f"         first {W} bytes of each row are the image (0x{GREY:02x}): "
          f"{set(image_part) == {GREY}}")
    print(f"         row 0, bytes {W}..{row} (past the row buffer):")
    for i in range(W, row, 32):
        print("           " + pixels[i : i + 32].hex())
    print(f"         {foreign} of {len(beyond)} bytes past the row buffers are neither "
          f"0x{GREY:02x} nor 0x00")
    leaked = foreign > 0


# --- Crash: EXIF says the image is 2**27 pixels wide ---------------------------------
child = subprocess.run(
    [sys.executable, __file__, "crash"],
    preexec_fn=lambda: resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_CORE, (0, 0)),  # no core file
    capture_output=True,
)
crashed = child.returncode in (-signal.SIGSEGV, -signal.SIGBUS)
outcome = signal.Signals(-child.returncode).name if child.returncode < 0 else "no signal"
print(f"crash:   child exit code {child.returncode} ({outcome})")


print("BUG" if control_clean and (leaked or crashed) else "OK")
```
</details>

advisories.summary: Hono: `csrf()` does not check requests sent by hyperlink auditing (`text/ping`)
advisories.description:
### Summary

`csrf()` validates a request only when its `Content-Type` is one of the three types an HTML form can send. Chromium's hyperlink auditing (`<a ping>`) sends a cross-origin POST with the user's cookies and the content type `text/ping`, which is not in that list. The middleware does not look at `Origin` or `Sec-Fetch-Site` for such a request, so it is passed to the handler.

### Details

The middleware skips the origin check when the content type is not one that a form submission produces. The assumption was that any other content type requires a CORS preflight and therefore cannot be sent cross-origin with credentials. Hyperlink auditing is an exception: Chrome and Edge send the ping as a credentialed POST without a preflight, with a fixed body and `Content-Type: text/ping`.

A page on another origin can therefore trigger a POST to any URL of the application. The `csrf()` options for `origin` and `secFetchSite` do not change the outcome, because neither header is evaluated for the request.

The request body is fixed, so only actions whose effect does not depend on the body can be triggered. Firefox does not send pings by default. As with any CSRF, the user's cookie must be sent with the request, which with the default `SameSite=Lax` means a same-site origin or a cookie set with `SameSite=None`.

### Impact

A user who visits a malicious page in Chrome or Edge while logged in to an application protected by `csrf()` can be made to send a state-changing request to that application, such as logging out, deleting a resource, or toggling a setting that is selected by the path or query string.

This issue affects applications that rely on `csrf()` as their CSRF protection and expose state-changing endpoints whose effect does not depend on the request body.

### Workarounds

Reject requests with a `Content-Type` of `text/ping` in a middleware registered before `csrf()`, or set session cookies with `SameSite=Strict`.

advisories.summary: Hono: `validator('form')` skips validation for `multipart/form-data` requests with extra parameters
advisories.description:
### Summary

`validator('form')` only recognizes a `multipart/form-data` `Content-Type` that carries nothing but a single `boundary` parameter. A request with another legal parameter, such as `charset`, or with extra whitespace after the `;` is not recognized as a form. The validation callback then receives an empty object, while `c.req.parseBody()` still parses the body as a form.

### Details

The check that decides whether a request body is a form was written as a strict pattern over the whole `Content-Type` value. Any parameter list that does not look exactly like `; boundary=...` fails the check. When it fails, the middleware does not read the body and passes an empty object to the validation callback. If the callback accepts an empty object, the request proceeds to the handler, which can still read all submitted fields through `c.req.parseBody()` or `c.req.formData()`.

`application/x-www-form-urlencoded` is not affected. Only the `multipart/form-data` branch has the strict pattern.

This issue arises when an application relies on `validator('form')` to reject or restrict fields and the validation callback does not fail on an empty object.

### Impact

An unauthenticated client can send form fields that the `form` validator never sees, by adding a legal parameter to the `Content-Type` header.

This may lead to:

- Allow-list or required-field checks in the validator being skipped
- Fields the application intended to reject reaching the handler

This issue affects applications that use `validator('form')` with `multipart/form-data` requests and whose validation callback accepts an empty object.

### Workarounds

Reject an empty object in the `validator('form')` callback, or validate the result of `await c.req.parseBody()` in the handler.

advisories.summary: Hono: `mount()` and `app.mount()` can forward a path that bypasses middleware scoped inside the mount prefix
advisories.description:
### Summary

`mount()` and `app.mount()` remove the mount prefix from the request path and forward the rest to the mounted application. Two mistakes in that step let a crafted request reach a route of the mounted application that the outer application protects with path-scoped middleware, such as an authentication check on `/app/admin/*`. The outer application routes on the original path, so the middleware does not run.

### Details

1. **Dynamic prefix** (all affected versions): for a mount such as `/api/:tenant/*`, the prefix was removed by the length of the route pattern, not of the matched prefix. A request with a longer or shorter first segment is cut in the middle, so `/api/a/xxxxx/admin/secret` reaches the mounted application as `/admin/secret`.
2. **Re-normalization** (since 4.12.21): the forwarded path was built from the decoded request path and assigned to `url.pathname`, which turns a decoded backslash into `/` and collapses `..`. `/app/public%5C..%5Cadmin/secret` reaches the mounted application as `/admin/secret`.

The fix removes the prefix segment by segment from the raw pathname, using the matched parameter values for its length. Route patterns that cannot be handled safely now throw: duplicate parameter names and a wildcard inside the last segment such as `/assets*`. A trailing slash in an `app.mount()` prefix no longer removes an extra segment.

### Impact

An unauthenticated client can reach a route of a mounted application that the outer application protects with path-scoped middleware.

This affects applications that use `mount()` or `app.mount()` and rely on middleware registered on a sub-path inside the mount prefix for authentication or authorization.

### Workarounds

Register the authentication middleware inside the mounted application.

cwes.name: Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel

advisories.summary: Hono: RegExpRouter skips wildcard middleware for some route sets and for paths with an encoded line terminator
advisories.description:
### Summary

RegExpRouter, which the default `SmartRouter` selects for most applications, skipped wildcard middleware in three cases, so a route handler ran without the middleware registered for it:

1. Middleware whose parameter is written with the explicit default pattern, such as `/api/:tenant{[^/]+}/admin/*`, was not applied to a route written as `/api/:tenant/admin/:id`. (since 4.13.0)
2. Middleware on `/admin/*` was not applied to a route registered on `/admin*` for paths under `/admin/`. (since 4.1.4)
3. For a path with an encoded line terminator (`%0A`, `%0D`, `%E2%80%A8`, `%E2%80%A9`), no wildcard pattern matched, so the request reached the not-found handler without any wildcard middleware. (since 4.4.0)

TrieRouter, LinearRouter and PatternRouter apply the middleware in all three cases.

### Details

RegExpRouter decides at registration time which wildcard middleware covers which route. In cases 1 and 2 it treated patterns that match the same requests as different ones. In case 3 the compiled wildcard did not match line terminators.

The fix derives the coverage from the structure of the registered paths and lets wildcards match line terminators. It also corrects other differences from the other routers (a wildcard in the middle of a path with parameters, duplicate middleware, middleware on static routes), and rejects custom patterns that can match the empty string, such as `{[0-9]*}`, with `UnsupportedPathError`. `PreparedRegExpRouter` data must be regenerated.

### Impact

An unauthenticated client can reach a route handler, or the not-found handler, without the authentication or authorization middleware registered on a wildcard path.

This affects applications that use RegExpRouter, directly or through the default `SmartRouter`, and rely on wildcard middleware for authentication or authorization.

### Workarounds

Use `new Hono({ router: new TrieRouter() })`.

advisories.summary: Hono: `css` helper does not escape a closing tag split between the template and an interpolated value, allowing HTML injection
advisories.description:
### Summary

The `css` helper in `hono/css` escapes a `/` that follows `<` inside an interpolated value so that a value cannot close the `<style>` element. The check only looks inside each value. When the text before a value ends with `<`, whether that is the template itself or an earlier interpolated value, and the next value starts with `/`, the `/` is not escaped and the combined output contains an unescaped closing tag.

### Details

Interpolated string values are escaped one at a time before they are joined with the surrounding template text. The rule that neutralizes `</` therefore cannot see a `<` that belongs to the template. A template such as a `content` declaration that opens with a literal `<` and interpolates a string right after it produces a raw `</style>` when that string starts with `/style>`. During server-side rendering the `<Style />` element is closed early and the rest of the value is interpreted as HTML.

This issue arises only when `<` is the last character before an interpolation in a `css` template, either written in the template or supplied by a preceding value, and the interpolated value is controlled by a client.

### Impact

A client that controls such a value can inject HTML, including script, into the page rendered on the server.

This may lead to:

- Execution of attacker-controlled script in the browser of a user who views the page
- Exposure of information available to that page

This issue affects applications that interpolate untrusted strings into a `css` template immediately after a `<`, including two adjacent interpolations such as `${prefix}${name}` where both are untrusted. Other uses of the `css` helper are not affected.

### Workarounds

Do not interpolate untrusted values into `css` templates, or make sure the text before an interpolated value does not end with `<`.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation

advisories.summary: @grpc/grpc-js: safe_regex incorrectly applies partial string matching for patterns with alternation
advisories.description:
### Summary

The StringMatcher/PathMatcher for `safe_regex` builds its RE2 as `^${regex}$` with no surrounding group. Because alternation has the lowest precedence, a pattern `"a|b|c"` compiles to `/^a|b|c$/` -- "starts with a" OR "contains b" OR "ends with c" instead of a full match of the whole value. Configurations with `safe_regex` matchers that use a regex alternation (a natural way to list methods or service identities) therefore apply partial string matches. This impacts route selection, xDS credentials, and RBAC.

### Details

`src/matcher.ts`: `SafeRegexValueMatcher` and `PathSafeRegexValueMatcher` both do
```ts
this.targetRegexImpl = new RE2(`^${targetRegex}$`, 'u');
```

and `apply()` returns `targetRegexImpl.test(value)`. With a top-level alternation the anchors bind only to the first/last branch.

https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/matcher.ts#L59

https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/matcher.ts#L232

`src/route.ts` (`getPredicateForStringMatcher` / `getPredicateForHeaderMatcher`) builds these for every `safe_regex` `StringMatcher`/`HeaderMatcher`, and src/rbac.ts uses them for RBAC `url_path` `permissions`/`principals`, `authenticated.principal_name` (mTLS SAN/CN), `requested_server_name` and `header rules`. So an ALLOW rule written with an alternation grants access to method names, certificate identities or header values that extend an intended one. DENY policies only become broader (fail-safe).

https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/route.ts#L28

https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/route.ts#L47

### Proof of concept

In a scratch directory:

```
npm init -y
npm i @grpc/grpc-js-xds@1.14.1 @grpc/grpc-js
node poc.cjs
```

`poc.cjs` calls the exported RBAC engine directly (the functions grpc-js uses to make the authorization decision); no server or network:

```js
const { parseConfig } = require('@grpc/grpc-js-xds/build/src/rbac.js')
const { SafeRegexValueMatcher } = require('@grpc/grpc-js-xds/build/src/matcher.js')
const { Metadata } = require('@grpc/grpc-js')

console.log(new SafeRegexValueMatcher('admin|editor').toString()) // SafeRegex(/^admin|editor$/u)

const sr = regex => ({ match_pattern: 'safe_regex', safe_regex: { regex } })
const info = urlPath => ({ urlPath, headers: new Metadata(), tls: true, peerCertificate: null,
  destinationIp: '10.0.0.1', destinationPort: 443, sourceIp: '10.0.0.2' })
const g = parseConfig({ action: 'ALLOW', policies: { p: {
  permissions: [{ rule: 'url_path', url_path: { path: sr('/acme.Users/GetUser|/acme.Users/ListUsers') } }],
  principals: [{ identifier: 'any', any: true }] } } })

console.log('GetUser       ', g.apply(info('/acme.Users/GetUser')))       // true  (intended)
console.log('DeleteUser    ', g.apply(info('/acme.Users/DeleteUser')))    // false (control)
console.log('GetUserSecrets', g.apply(info('/acme.Users/GetUserSecrets'))) // true <-- BYPASS
```

Observed (grpc-js-xds 1.14.1, grpc-js 1.14.6):

```
matcher "admin|editor" -> SafeRegex(/^admin|editor$/u);
    apply("administrator")=true, apply("not-an-editor")=true
ALLOW url_path /acme.Users/GetUser|/acme.Users/ListUsers:
    /acme.Users/GetUser         -> ALLOWED (intended)
    /acme.Users/DeleteUser      -> denied  (control)
    /acme.Users/GetUserSecrets  -> ALLOWED <-- bypass (policy intends deny)
control, same regex as (?:...|...): /acme.Users/GetUserSecrets -> denied
ALLOW authenticated principal_name spiffe://prod/ns/web/sa/frontend|...ops/sa/admin:
    spiffe://prod/ns/web/sa/frontend-batch -> ALLOWED <-- bypass
```

### Impact

Users of `@grpc/grpc-js-xds` who are using `safe_regex` matchers with alternation for route selection, xDS credentials SAN matchers, or RBAC rules may see incorrectly permissive behavior.

advisories.summary: @grpc/grpc-js: RBAC override configs in VirtualHost and Route resources are not applied
advisories.description:
### Summary

`XdsServer` in `@grpc/grpc-js-xds` does not apply `RBACPerRoute` overrides from matching Route or VirtualHost resources. When a trusted xDS control plane supplies a broad top-level ALLOW policy and a stricter override, `XdsServer` ACKs the resources but evaluates the RPC under the top-level policy.

### Details

### Override parser lookup uses the override message type

`parseOverrideFilterConfig()` in packages/grpc-js-xds/src/http-filter.ts:225-257 looks up FILTER_REGISTRY using the override message type:

`type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.rbac.v3.RBACPerRoute`
Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/http-filter.ts#L225-L257

`setup()` in packages/grpc-js-xds/src/http-filter/rbac-filter.ts:167-173 registers the filter only under the top-level RBAC type:

`type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.rbac.v3.RBAC`
Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/http-filter/rbac-filter.ts#L167-L173

The lookup returns null even though the registered entry contains `parseOverrideRbacConfig()`, and server.ts silently skips the override.

### Override maps are keyed by type URL instead of filter name

`overrideConfigMaps` in server.ts:99-102 is documented as keyed by HTTP filter name, but server.ts:169-174 stores each map under `filterConfig.typeUrl`.

Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/server.ts#L99-L102

Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/server.ts#L169-L174

Route overrides are later looked up by their `typed_per_filter_config` key, which is the `HttpFilter.name`. An ordinary key such as rbac therefore misses the stored map.

### VirtualHost overrides are not read

`handleRouteConfigurationResource()` in server.ts:225-249 reads `route.typed_per_filter_config` but never reads `virtualHost.typed_per_filter_config`.

Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/server.ts#L225-L249

When no override reaches the RBAC interceptor, rbac-filter.ts:125-155 evaluates the broader top-level policy.

### Proof of concept

Set:
```
GRPC_XDS_EXPERIMENTAL_RBAC=true
```

Run `XdsServer` with a protected unary handler.

Have the ADS control plane deliver a Listener containing an RBAC HTTP filter named rbac with a top-level ALLOW-any policy:

```
name: rbac
typed_config:
  "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.rbac.v3.RBAC
  rules:
    action: ALLOW
    policies:
      allow-any:
        principals: [{ any: true }]
        permissions: [{ any: true }]
```

Deliver a matching non-forwarding route with this override:

```
typed_per_filter_config:
  rbac:
    "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.rbac.v3.RBACPerRoute
    rbac:
      rules:
        action: DENY
        policies:
          deny-any:
            principals: [{ any: true }]
            permissions: [{ any: true }]
```

Invoke the protected unary method without credentials.

Expected: The route-specific DENY policy rejects the RPC before the protected handler runs.

Observed: `XdsServer` ACKs the resources, retains the top-level ALLOW policy, and runs the protected handler.

```
Listener and RouteConfiguration: ACKED
gRPC status: OK
handler invocations: 1
response: PROTECTED_SECRET_RECORD_RBAC_OVERRIDE
```

### Impact

Users of `@grpc/grpc-js-xds` who are using RBAC-based authentication with override configurations may unintentionally accept some requests that should be rejected.

advisories.summary: msgpack-ruby JRuby decoder makes uncapped header-count allocations; a 5-byte message forces multi-GiB OOM
advisories.description:
### Summary

The **JRuby** implementation of msgpack (`msgpack` gem, `java` platform — pure Java decoder under `ext/java/`) sizes containers directly from the element count written in the message header, with **no cap at all**: no equivalent of the C unpacker's `SHRT_MAX` clamp (since 1.7.3) and none of the buffered-bytes cap that commit c8d42d8 added for CRuby in 1.8.6. A single 5-byte message decides how much memory a JVM process tries to allocate:

* `array32` header declaring `0x7FFFFFFF` elements → `new IRubyObject[0x7FFFFFFF]` (~8 GiB of reference slots) attempted immediately → `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Requested array size exceeds VM limit`.
* Counts *below* the VM's max-array-size but above available heap (e.g. 5×10⁸ with a 512 MiB heap) produce a **real allocation attempt** — `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` — the JVM genuinely tries to take the memory before failing.
* `str32`/`bin32` headers declaring `0x7FFFFFFF` bytes do the same via `readBytes(size)` → `new byte[size]`.
* Below the failure threshold there is a **silent band**: one streaming unpacker fed only an `array32` header with count 2×10⁷ (5 wire bytes, zero elements) grows used heap **+78 MiB immediately**, no exception (`each` swallows the underflow), and the footprint stays elevated after `Unpacker#reset` + full GC. Linear in declared count (~4 B/element); nothing bounds it — not delivered bytes, not a per-container cap.

Only counts ≥ 2³¹ are refused (a clean `MessagePack::UnderflowError` from `getUnsignedInt()`), and only **maps** are safe (`consumeHash` grows per element instead of pre-sizing). Verified on the released gem `msgpack 1.8.6 java`, JRuby 9.4.12 / OpenJDK 25, 2026-10-30 — i.e. **unfixed in the current release**. Proposed fix mirrors c8d42d8: cap initial allocation by bytes actually buffered and grow as data arrives; read strings in bounded chunks instead of allocating the declared length up front.


### Details

### 1. The four dispatch arms, and which pre-allocate (line numbers at tag v1.8.6 — current release; `ext/java` has no commits after it)

| header | dispatch ([Decoder.java](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java)) | behaviour on the declared count | measured (released 1.8.6-java, Xmx512m) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `array32` `\xdd` | [:296](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L296) → [`consumeArray(int size)` :139-145](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L139-L145) | `new IRubyObject[size]` **immediately**, before reading any element | count `0x7FFFFFFF`: OOME "Requested array size exceeds VM limit"; count 5×10⁸: OOME "**Java heap space**" (real allocation attempt); count 2×10⁷: **+78 MiB, silent** |
| `str32` `\xdb` | [:294](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L294) → [`consumeString` :129](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L129) → [`readBytes(int size)` :186-190](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L186-L190) | `new byte[size]` **immediately** | len `0x7FFFFFFF`: OOME "array size exceeds VM limit" |
| `bin32` `\xc6` | [:269](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L269) → same `consumeString`/`readBytes` | same | len `0x7FFFFFFF`: OOME "array size exceeds VM limit" |
| `map32` `\xdf` | [:298](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L298) → [`consumeHash(int size)` :147+](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L147) | **no pre-allocation** — inserts per element, underflows on first missing byte | count `0x7FFFFFFF`: no exception (swallowed), no large allocation |

The only guard is [`getUnsignedInt()` :88-94](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L88-L94): counts with the top bit set (≥ 2³¹) raise `MessagePack::UnderflowError: Size too large (limited to 2**31 for the Java version)`. That bounds the *value* but leaves the entire positive band `(available heap, 2³¹)` unbounded — and that band is where real allocation attempts happen.

### 2. Contrast with the C implementation (same repo)

The CRuby unpacker has had a per-container cap since 1.7.3 (`INITIAL_BUFFER_CAPACITY_MAX = SHRT_MAX`) and, since [c8d42d8](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/commit/c8d42d8) in **1.8.6**, additionally caps initial size by bytes actually buffered ("an element needs at least one byte…"). Strings on C are bounded too (`read_raw_body_cont` allocates `min(remaining, buffered)`). The Java decoder has **neither generation of cap** — it is strictly behind the CRuby behaviour this repo already considers correct enough to ship.

### 3. Silent retention + mechanism control (measured 2026-10-30, released gem)

One `MessagePack::Unpacker` per process, fed only a header (`"\xdd" + [count].pack('N')`), zero elements; heap = `Runtime.total_memory - free_memory` after `GC.start` on both sides:

| declared count | used heap before → after | delta | exception? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1,000,000 | 26.4 → 31.1 MiB | +4.7 | none (`each` swallows the underflow) |
| 5,000,000 | 53.3 → 74.0 MiB | +20.7 | none |
| 20,000,000 | 51.3 → 129.3 MiB | **+78.0** | none |

Mechanism control: after the feed, `Unpacker#reset` + three `GC.start` cycles left used heap at **+79.4 MiB above baseline** (2×10⁷ arm) — the elevation is *not* unpacker-held state; it is JVM heap already spent on header-declared allocation and not returned. Either way the process footprint grows per attack and stays grown; the peak cost is paid synchronously during parsing regardless of GC behaviour afterwards. (Honest scope note: this is unbounded **allocation**, not a memory leak.)

### 4. Why JVM makes availability impact worse than the CRuby analogue

In CRuby, allocation failure raises `NoMemoryError`/fails inside one worker process. In a JVM, an OOME raised on the parser thread can land anywhere in the host application's shared runtime — long-lived JRuby servers (Rails, Logstash-class pipelines, JDBC apps) share heap across all threads and connections; a single crafted message can destabilize or kill the whole JVM, not just the request. The silent band means no exception at all is even required to spend memory.

### 5. Not claimed / scope

* **Fluentd is NOT affected** (and this report deliberately does not involve it): Fluentd ships CRuby-only — CI pins `engine: cruby`, gemspec requires ruby >= 3.3 while JRuby 9.4 implements Ruby 3.1 semantics, and there are zero JRUBY guards in lib/. This is an upstream msgpack-ruby report only.
* Maps (`map32`) do not pre-allocate — measured; the class applies to `array32`/`str32`/`bin32`.
* Counts ≥ 2³¹ are cleanly refused — measured; no claim there.
* Older java-gem releases were not individually probed; `<= 1.8.6` means "every release up to the current one carries this code".


### Proof of concept

Verified on the **released gem** `msgpack 1.8.6 java`, JRuby 9.4.12.0, OpenJDK 25.0.4.1, Linux x86-64 (artifacts in `evidence_186_recheck/`). Always run with a small `-Xmx` so oversized requests fail fast instead of wrecking the box.

### Setup

```console
$ curl -fsSLO https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/org/jruby/jruby-dist/9.4.12.0/jruby-dist-9.4.12.0-bin.tar.gz
$ tar xzf jruby-dist-9.4.12.0-bin.tar.gz && export PATH=$PWD/jruby-9.4.12.0/bin:$PATH
$ jruby -S gem install msgpack --no-document      # resolves the java-platform gem: "msgpack (1.8.6 java)"
```

### 1. Header shapes (fresh process per arm, `-Xmx512m`)

```console
array32 count=0xFFFFFFFF       -> MessagePack::UnderflowError: Size too large (limited to 2**31 for the Java version)
array32 count=0x7FFFFFFF       -> Java::JavaLang::OutOfMemoryError: Requested array size exceeds VM limit
array32 count=500000000        -> Java::JavaLang::OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space   # real allocation attempt
str32   len=0x7FFFFFFF         -> Java::JavaLang::OutOfMemoryError: Requested array size exceeds VM limit
bin32   len=0x7FFFFFFF         -> Java::JavaLang::OutOfMemoryError: Requested array size exceeds VM limit
map32   count=0x7FFFFFFF       -> no exception, no large allocation (consumeHash grows per element)
```

Each payload is five bytes, e.g. `"\xdd" + [count].pack('N')` fed to `MessagePack::Unpacker#feed_each`. Scripts: `jr_probe.rb`, `jr_probe_extra.rb` (attached in kit).

### 2. Silent band — retention from one header (Xmx1g)

```console
$ for n in 1000000 5000000 20000000; do jruby -J-Xmx1g jr_one.rb $n; done
count=  1000000 heap 26.4 -> 31.1 MiB (delta 4.7)   | no exception (underflow swallowed)
count=  5000000 heap 53.3 -> 74.0 MiB (delta 20.7)  | no exception (underflow swallowed)
count= 20000000 heap 51.3 -> 129.3 MiB (delta 78.0) | no exception (underflow swallowed)

$ jruby -J-Xmx1g jr_reset_control.rb 20000000
count=20000000 heap base=49.9 after_feed=129.3 (delta 79.4) after_reset_gc=129.3 (retained_vs_base 79.4)
```

A streaming server that keeps one unpacker per connection (the pattern any socket-fed msgpack service uses) pays this per connection with five wire bytes each and produces no exception, no log line.

### 3. Fix verification path

Apply the C-side idea from c8d42d8: in `consumeArray`, cap the initial array by bytes actually buffered (an element needs ≥ 1 byte) and grow as elements arrive; in `readBytes`/`consumeString`, read in bounded chunks instead of allocating the declared length up front. Then re-run this PoC: the silent band should track delivered bytes, and oversized declarations should raise `UnderflowError`-class errors without touching multi-GiB allocations. msgpack-ruby CI runs jruby-9.4/truffleruby, so a patch is verifiable as-is; I can prepare one against `ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java`.


### Impact

**Type.** Uncontrolled resource consumption driven by *declared* sizes rather than delivered bytes — CWE-770 (Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling), precisely CWE-1325 (Independent Resource Usage Limiting Not Applied). Availability only; no confidentiality/integrity impact, no code execution.

**Who is impacted.** Any JRuby application that feeds untrusted msgpack to `MessagePack.unpack`/`Unpacker` — the java-platform gem's whole user base (JRuby-based services, log/RPC pipelines, JVM polyglot stacks using this gem). For them: remote OOM of a shared-heap JVM from a 5-byte message, or silent heap spend below the exception band.

**Severity.** Proposed **High / 7.5**, `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H` — remote, trivially crafted, default settings, process death; same metric string as the accepted fluentd OOM family (e.g. GHSA-h3xv-5jpx-r4j2) and as this repo's own C-side analogue (reported separately, patched at 1.8.6). If triage weighs the platform scope (java gem only), lower framings read against that — we flag it honestly; the maintainers' call on scope shouldn't delay the patch.

**Relationship to the C-side report.** Same flaw class, different implementation and fix state: CRuby's pre-allocation was capped by c8d42d8 (released 1.8.6, separate advisory with affected `<= 1.8.5`, patched `1.8.6`). This JRuby variant is **unfixed in 1.8.6** and needs its own patch + CVE. Cross-reference both ways once filed.

**What this is not.** Not a Fluentd issue (Fluentd is CRuby-only — CI pins cruby, gemspec ruby >= 3.3 vs JRuby's Ruby 3.1 semantics); no fluentd advisory should carry this. Not a memory leak (measured: footprint elevation persists after reset+GC without retained objects). Not exploitable via maps or counts ≥ 2³¹ (both measured safe/cleanly refused).

advisories.summary: Addressable display_uri can show misleading hosts with invalid Punycode A-labels
advisories.description:
### Impact

`Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode`, in the pure-Ruby IDNA implementation, decodes Punycode labels (labels beginning with `xn--`) that are not valid A-labels. Those labels are returned in decoded form, when they should be returned unchanged. That includes:

- labels that decode to only ASCII characters, e.g. `xn--google-` decodes to `google`;
- labels that decode to text that doesn't convert back to the same label (RFC 3490 §4.2), e.g. text that isn't in normalized form.

`Addressable::URI#display_uri` uses `to_unicode`, so for `https://xn--google-.example.org/` it displays the host `google.example.org`, while `#host`, `#normalized_host` and any connection made from the URI use `xn--google-.example.org`. An attacker who controls a domain can therefore have a URI displayed as a host they don't control. Applications that compare the result of `to_unicode` against a list of trusted names can likewise treat two different hosts as the same.

The native IDNA implementation, used when libidn and the `idn-ruby` gem are installed, is not affected. `to_ascii` and `normalized_host` are not affected.

### Affected Versions

This vulnerability affects Addressable >= 2.0.0, the first version with the pure-Ruby IDNA implementation, when that implementation is in use. It is fixed in 2.9.1, where such labels are returned unchanged, as with libidn.

### Workarounds

- Install libidn and the `idn-ruby` gem, so that Addressable uses the native IDNA implementation.
- Don't make security decisions on `display_uri` or `to_unicode` output. Compare hosts using `normalized_host`.

### Credits

Reported by @tonghuaroot.

### For more information

If there are any questions or comments about this advisory:
* [Open an issue](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/issues)

advisories.summary: Addressable display_uri can show misleading hosts containing bidi and invisible characters
advisories.description:
### Impact

`Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode` decodes Punycode labels (labels beginning with `xn--`) that contain characters which change how text is displayed without being visible themselves. These include bidirectional controls such as U+202E RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE and U+2066–U+2069, zero-width characters, and other invisible format characters. `Addressable::URI#display_uri` uses `to_unicode`, so it can display a host whose characters appear reordered or which looks identical to a different host. For example, the host of `http://xn--abcmoc-dm0c.com/` is displayed as `abc`, U+202E, `moc.com`, and the override makes everything after `abc` render right to left.

Parsing, `host`, `normalized_host` and any connection made from the URI are not affected. Only the displayed form is. Applications that show `display_uri` to users (link previews, chat and email clients, admin interfaces) can be used to make a malicious domain look like a trusted one.

- In the pure-Ruby IDNA implementation, all such characters are decoded, including those that IDNA's nameprep profile prohibits.
- In the native IDNA implementation, used when libidn and the `idn-ruby` gem are installed, libidn rejects most of them, but not characters added to Unicode after version 3.2, such as U+061C and U+2066–U+2069.

### Affected Versions

The pure-Ruby IDNA implementation is affected in Addressable >= 2.0.0. The native IDNA implementation is affected in Addressable >= 2.5.2, when `to_unicode` began accepting characters unassigned in Unicode 3.2. It is fixed in 2.9.1 for both implementations, where such labels are returned unchanged.

### Workarounds

- Install libidn and the `idn-ruby` gem, so that Addressable uses the native IDNA implementation. This reduces the affected characters to those added since Unicode 3.2.
- Check displayed hosts for bidirectional and invisible characters (e.g., `/[\p{Cc}\p{Cf}\p{Default_Ignorable_Code_Point}]/`) and fall back to `normalized_host` when one is present.

### Credits

Reported by @andrewstellman.

### For more information

If there are any questions or comments about this advisory:
* [Open an issue](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/issues)

advisories.summary: Addressable: Denial of service in URI path normalization
advisories.description:
### Impact

`Addressable::URI.normalize_path` takes time quadratic in the number of nested dot segments in a path (e.g., `"/" + "a/" * n + "../" * n`, which for n = 3 is `/a/a/a/../../../`), because it removes one dot segment per pass over the whole path. `URI#normalize`, `URI#normalized_path`, `URI#==`, `URI#===` and `URI#join` all call it. Normalizing, comparing or joining a URI taken from user input can result in uncontrolled resource consumption, leading to denial of service. On 2.9.0, normalizing a 34 KB path takes about 3.5 seconds on MRI Ruby 4.0, and the cost grows with the square of the path length.

This affects every Ruby implementation, including MRI Ruby 3.2 and later. `URI.parse` by itself is unaffected, as is code that never normalizes, compares, or joins URIs from untrusted sources.

### Affected Versions

This vulnerability affects all versions of Addressable prior to 2.9.1. It is fixed in 2.9.1.

### Workarounds

- Limit the length of URIs taken from user input before calling `normalize`, `==` or `join` on them. Web servers often limit request lines to about 8 KB, which keeps the cost to about 150 milliseconds per call on typical hardware, but URIs from other sources (request bodies, headers such as `Location`, stored data) may not be limited.
- Reject paths with many dot segments before normalizing them.

### Credits

Reported by Matthew Mongeau (@halogenandtoast), Ruby Central Gem Security, who also suggested the single-pass approach used in the fix.

### For more information

If there are any questions or comments about this advisory:
* [Open an issue](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/issues)

advisories.summary: Astro: Reflected XSS via unescaped slot names in @astrojs/solid-js
advisories.description:
## Summary The `@astrojs/solid-js` renderer wraps named slot content passed to Solid components in an `` element, and writes the slot name into its `name` attribute without HTML escaping. A slot name containing `"` could end the attribute and inject arbitrary HTML into the page. For example, a page that takes a slot name from the request: ```astro --- import Tabs from '../components/Tabs.jsx'; const tab = Astro.url.searchParams.get('tab'); ---
…
 ``` rendered with a Solid component that renders a slot by name: ```jsx export default function Tabs(props) { return
{props[props.active]}
; } ``` would output a `tab` value such as `x">` as live HTML. ## Impact Reflected cross-site scripting. An attacker who gets a user to open a crafted link can run JavaScript on the site's origin, but only in applications where all of the following are true: - The page passes request-controlled input (such as a query parameter) as a slot name. - The Solid component is hydrated with a `client:*` directive. For non-hydrated components the slot wrapper is removed from the output, together with its `name` attribute. - The Solid component renders the attacker-chosen slot, which in practice means accessing slot props by a dynamic name. Components that never render the slot only output Astro's already escaped fallback template. This is the `@astrojs/solid-js` counterpart of GHSA-8hv8-536x-4wqp (CVE-2026-50146), which fixed the same issue in `astro` core. ## Affected versions `@astrojs/solid-js` >= 0.2.0, <= 7.1.1. ## Patches Fixed in `@astrojs/solid-js` 7.1.2. Slot names are now HTML-escaped in the server renderer. ## Workarounds Upgrade to `@astrojs/solid-js` 7.1.2 or later. Before upgrading, do not use request-controlled input as a slot name, or map it to a fixed set of known slot names before passing it to a component. ## Credits Reported by @manus-pi.

advisories.summary: Astro: Reflected XSS via unescaped slot names in @astrojs/svelte
advisories.description:
## Summary The `@astrojs/svelte` renderer wraps slotted content passed to Svelte components in an `` element, and writes the slot name into its `name` attribute without HTML escaping. A slot name containing `"` could end the attribute and inject arbitrary HTML into the page. For example, a page that takes a slot name from the request: ```astro --- import Tabs from '../components/Tabs.svelte'; const tab = Astro.url.searchParams.get('tab'); ---
…
 ``` rendered with a Svelte 5 component that renders its snippets by name: ```svelte {@render snippets[active]?.()} ``` would output a `tab` value such as `x">` as live HTML. ## Impact Reflected cross-site scripting. An attacker who gets a user to open a crafted link can run JavaScript on the site's origin, but only in applications where all of the following are true: - The page passes request-controlled input (such as a query parameter) as a slot name. - The Svelte component is hydrated with a `client:*` directive. For non-hydrated components the slot wrapper is removed from the output, together with its `name` attribute. - The Svelte component renders the attacker-chosen slot, which in practice means a Svelte 5 component that renders snippets by a dynamic name. Components that never render the slot only output Astro's already escaped fallback template. This is the `@astrojs/svelte` counterpart of GHSA-8hv8-536x-4wqp (CVE-2026-50146), which fixed the same issue in `astro` core. The same unescaped value was also used when hydrating the component in the browser. ## Affected versions `@astrojs/svelte` >= 5.7.3, <= 9.1.1. ## Patches Fixed in `@astrojs/svelte` 9.1.2. Slot names are now HTML-escaped in the server renderer and in the client-side hydration code. ## Workarounds Upgrade to `@astrojs/svelte` 9.1.2 or later. Before upgrading, do not use request-controlled input as a slot name, or map it to a fixed set of known slot names before passing it to a component. ## Credits Reported by @manus-pi.

advisories.summary: Addressable: Regular Expression Denial of Service in templates with certain exploded expressions
advisories.description:
### Impact

Within the URI template implementation in Addressable, templates using the `*` (explode) modifier with the `/`, `.`, `;`, `?` or `&` operators (e.g., `{/segments*}`, `{.ext*}`, `{;params*}`, `{?query*}`) generate regular expressions vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking. When `Template#match` or `Template#extract` is called with a maliciously crafted URI that starts with the operator's leading character, matching takes exponential time, leading to uncontrolled resource consumption and denial of service. An input under 60 bytes is enough to occupy a thread for minutes.

GHSA-h27x-rffw-24p4 (CVE-2026-35611) reported this pattern as fully remediated in 2.9.0. The 2.9.0 fix only made the joiner between exploded members mandatory for templates without an operator, and its regression specs used inputs that never start with the operator's leading character, so the vulnerable part of the expression was never reached. This issue was originally reported in #364 by @ebenoist in 2019 but insufficiently investigated.

Users of the URI parsing capabilities in Addressable but not the URI template matching capabilities are unaffected. Users who only call `Template#expand` are unaffected.

### Affected Versions

This vulnerability affects Addressable >= 2.3.0 (note: 2.3.0 and 2.3.1 were yanked; the earliest installable release is 2.3.2), including 2.9.0. It is fixed in 2.9.1.

The vulnerability is only exploitable on Ruby implementations whose regular expression engine backtracks without memoization: MRI Ruby < 3.2 and JRuby. MRI Ruby 3.2 and later are not affected: their regular expression engine memoizes backtracking, so these patterns still match in linear time. TruffleRuby 40.0 is not affected either. Earlier TruffleRuby versions were not tested.

This has been confirmed on the following runtimes with Addressable 2.9.0:

| Runtime | Status |
|---------|--------|
| MRI Ruby 2.7 | Vulnerable |
| MRI Ruby 3.1 | Vulnerable |
| MRI Ruby 3.2 | Not affected |
| MRI Ruby 3.3 | Not affected |
| MRI Ruby 3.4 | Not affected |
| MRI Ruby 4.0 | Not affected |
| JRuby 9.4 | Vulnerable |
| TruffleRuby 40.0 | Not affected |

### Workarounds

- Upgrade to MRI Ruby 3.2 or later, if the consuming application does not use JRuby.
- Avoid matching user-supplied input on unpatched versions of the library against templates that use the `*` modifier with the `/`, `.`, `;`, `?` or `&` operators.
- Apply a short timeout around any call to `Template#match` or `Template#extract` that processes user-supplied data.

### Credits

Reported independently by @ebenoist, @andrewstellman, and then @halogenandtoast.

### For more information

If there are any questions or comments about this advisory:
* [Open an issue](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/issues)

advisories.summary: Addressable: Regular Expression Denial of Service in templates with multiple variables
advisories.description:
### Impact

Within the URI template implementation in Addressable, templates that put several variables in one expression generate regular expressions vulnerable to excessive backtracking:

1. Expressions with any operator other than `+` and `#` (e.g., `{/owner,repo,ref}`, `{.a,b}`, `{a,b,c}`, `{;a,b,c}`). The values are joined by an optional separator, so a run of characters can be divided among the variables in O(n^k) ways for k variables.
2. Expressions with the `+` or `#` operators and many variables (e.g., `{+v1,v2,v3,v4,v5,v6,v7,v8,v9,v10}`). A failing match is exponential in the number of variables.
3. Several single-variable expressions next to each other (e.g., `{+a}{+b}{+c}` or `{a}{b}{c}`), which are polynomial in the input length.

When `Template#match` or `Template#extract` is called with a maliciously crafted URI, this can result in uncontrolled resource consumption, leading to denial of service. A three-variable path template such as `http://example.com/repos{/owner,repo,ref}` needs about 2 KB of input to occupy a thread for many seconds.

Users of the URI parsing capabilities in Addressable but not the URI template matching capabilities are unaffected. Users who only call `Template#expand` are unaffected.

### Affected Versions

This vulnerability affects Addressable >= 2.3.0 (note: 2.3.0 and 2.3.1 were yanked; the earliest installable release is 2.3.2), including 2.9.0. It is fixed in 2.9.1.

The vulnerability is exploitable on Ruby implementations whose regular expression engine backtracks without memoization: MRI Ruby < 3.2 and JRuby. The second form, many-variable `+` and `#` expressions, is also exploitable on MRI Ruby 3.2, which does not memoize a regular expression that contains possessive quantifiers, and 2.9.0 generates those for these operators. It is also exploitable on TruffleRuby 40.0, whose regular expression engine falls back to backtracking for them. MRI Ruby 3.3 and later are not affected by any form, because they memoize those regular expressions too. TruffleRuby 40.0 is not affected by the other two forms. Earlier TruffleRuby versions were not tested.

This has been confirmed on the following runtimes with Addressable 2.9.0:

| Runtime | Status |
|---------|--------|
| MRI Ruby 2.7 | Vulnerable |
| MRI Ruby 3.1 | Vulnerable |
| MRI Ruby 3.2 | Vulnerable |
| MRI Ruby 3.3 | Not affected |
| MRI Ruby 3.4 | Not affected |
| MRI Ruby 4.0 | Not affected |
| JRuby 9.4 | Vulnerable |
| JRuby 10.1 | Vulnerable |
| TruffleRuby 40.0 | Vulnerable |

### Workarounds

- Upgrade to MRI Ruby 3.3 or later, if a consuming application does not use JRuby or TruffleRuby.
- Avoid matching user-supplied input on unpatched versions of the library against templates with several variables in one expression, or with several expressions next to each other.
- Apply a short timeout around any call to `Template#match` or `Template#extract` that processes user-supplied data.

### Credits

Reported by Matthew Mongeau (@halogenandtoast), Ruby Central Gem Security.

### For more information

If there are any questions or comments about this advisory:
* [Open an issue](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/issues)

advisories.summary: Addressable URI normalization resolves some dotted path segments to the wrong path
advisories.description:
### Summary

`Addressable::URI.normalize_path` resolves some paths containing `..` segments to a different path than RFC 3986 does. When a path climbs above the root before any other `..` is resolved, the segments that later `..` segments should remove are instead kept: `/../../public/x/../../secret` normalizes to `/public/x/secret` instead of `/secret`. `URI#normalize`, `URI#join`, `URI#==` and `URI#===` all use this normalization. An application that checks a normalized Addressable path against an allowlist, but sends the original URI to something that resolves it according to RFC 3986, can be made to allow a request for a path outside the allowlist.

### Details

`normalize_path` in 2.9.0 (`lib/addressable/uri.rb`) removes dot segments by repeating a set of rewrites until nothing changes. On each pass it finds the first `/segment/../` pair with `RULE_2B_2C`, then replaces every textual copy of that pair in the path with `/`:

```ruby
pair = normalized_path.match(RULE_2B_2C)
...
regexp = "/#{Regexp.escape(parent.to_s)}/\\.\\./|"
regexp += "(/#{Regexp.escape(current.to_s)}/\\.\\.$)"
...
mod ||= normalized_path.gsub!(Regexp.new(regexp), SLASH)
```

When the first pair found is `/../../`, where the "segment" is itself `..`, every `/../../` in the path is replaced with `/`. That includes copies later in the path, where each `..` should have removed the segment before it. For `/../../public/x/../../secret`:

- RFC 3986 §5.2.4 drops the two leading `..` segments, which can't go above the root, then removes `x` and `public`, giving `/secret`.
- 2.9.0 replaces both copies of `/../../` with `/` in one step, giving `/public/x/secret`.

Paths where an ordinary `/segment/../` pair comes first, such as `/a/../../b/c/../../d`, are resolved correctly.

This was introduced in 2.2.5. Versions 2.0.0 through 2.2.4 and earlier versions resolve these paths correctly. It is fixed in 2.9.1, which replaces the rewrite loop with a single pass that correctly follows RFC 3986 §5.2.4.

### Proof of concept

```ruby
require "addressable/uri"
require "uri"

url = "http://example.com/../../public/x/../../secret"

# Addressable's normalized path, compared with RFC 3986 resolution by Ruby's URI library
puts Addressable::URI.parse(url).normalize.path
puts URI.join("http://example.com/", "../../public/x/../../secret").path

# join and == use the same normalization
puts Addressable::URI.join("http://example.com/", "../../public/x/../../secret").path
puts Addressable::URI.parse(url) == Addressable::URI.parse("http://example.com/public/x/secret")

# An allowlist check on the normalized path passes, but the request reaches /secret
def allowed?(url) = Addressable::URI.parse(url).normalize.path.start_with?("/public/")
puts allowed?(url)
```

Output with Addressable 2.9.0:

```
/public/x/secret
/secret
/public/x/secret
true
true
```

Output with Addressable 2.9.1:

```
/secret
/secret
/secret
false
false
```


### Impact

This is an interpretation conflict (CWE-436) between Addressable and other RFC 3986 resolvers, which could lead to path traversal past an allowlist (CWE-22). An application is affected when it does both of these:

- makes an access decision on a path normalized or joined by Addressable, such as "only paths under `/public/` may be proxied" or "only these redirect targets are allowed";
- sends the original, unnormalized URI to a component that resolves dot segments itself, such as an HTTP client, a proxy, a web server or a browser.

An attacker may be able to bypass a check by exploiting behavioral differences between URI parsers. Impact from this is application-dependent. Applications that use Addressable's normalized form for both the check and the request are unaffected, as are applications that reject paths containing `..` segments.

As a work-around for unpatched versions, before making access decisions on a path, either reject any containing `..` segments, including percent-encoded forms such as `%2e%2e`, or use the same normalized value for both the check and the request.

advisories.summary: basic-ftp: Uncaught exception crashes the Node.js process when a password (or resumed-download path) contains CR/LF
Action View: Possible XSS vulnerability in tag helpers
advisories.description:
### Impact
The fix for [CVE-2026-33168](https://github.com/rails/rails/security/advisories/GHSA-v55j-83pf-r9cq) skips blank HTML attribute names in Action View tag helpers, but it tests the name before converting it to a string. A Symbol name made only of whitespace, such as `:" "`, is not blank, because `Symbol#blank?` is `Symbol#empty?`, so it reaches the attribute escaping, which emits an attribute with no name and produces malformed HTML. The asset tag helpers, such as `image_tag`, `video_tag` and `audio_tag`, symbolize their options, so a whitespace String name passed to them takes the same path. A carefully crafted attribute value could then be misinterpreted by the browser as a separate attribute name, possibly leading to XSS. Applications that allow users to specify custom HTML attribute names are affected.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/9190210606ffe52f92fdc75637f8ff69404f22c8.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/f47452533e1f28d847c63181b9d5f8b7243ef9a4.patch

### Credit
This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher [thepo1es](https://hackerone.com/thepo1es).

advisories.summary: Active Storage: Possible local file disclosure in video previews and analysis
advisories.description:
### Impact
Active Storage's `VideoPreviewer`, `VideoAnalyzer` and `AudioAnalyzer` run `ffmpeg` and `ffprobe` on a blob's contents without restricting the input format, so FFmpeg selects a demuxer by probing the file. A blob created through a direct upload keeps the content type the client declared, so a client can store an HLS playlist under a `video/*` or `audio/*` type. When that blob is previewed or analyzed, the `hls` demuxer opens the `file://` segments that the playlist names, and the preview image or the stored metadata could disclose a local media file that the application process can read and whose path the attacker knows.

Applications that accept uploads from untrusted users and generate video previews, or analyze video or audio attachments with FFmpeg, are affected.

### Details
The fixed releases limit the formats FFmpeg may open to common audio and video containers, configured by the new `config.active_storage.ffmpeg_allowed_formats` setting. Files in other formats no longer preview or receive media metadata; the Active Storage CHANGELOG names some of them and shows how to add a format to the list.

### Workarounds
Applications that cannot upgrade can stop Active Storage from running FFmpeg on uploaded files by removing `ActiveStorage::Previewer::VideoPreviewer` from `config.active_storage.previewers`, and `ActiveStorage::Analyzer::VideoAnalyzer` and `ActiveStorage::Analyzer::AudioAnalyzer` from `config.active_storage.analyzers`.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
