advisories.summary: The MISP Modules website component contains an information disclosure vulnerability in the...
advisories.description:
The MISP Modules website component contains an information disclosure vulnerability in the external tools management interface. The /external_tools/list endpoint returned stored API keys (the api_key field) in its JSON response via the ExternalTools model serializer. Additionally, the browser-based edit form pre-populated the API key input field with the stored credential value, exposing it in the DOM.

The /external_tools/list endpoint is accessible without authentication (the regression tests verify the response for both authenticated and unauthenticated clients), meaning any network-reachable client could retrieve the API keys for all configured external tools. These keys are used by the server to authenticate submissions to external analysis or enrichment services, so their disclosure allows an attacker to impersonate the MISP instance or directly access those external services.

The vulnerability also affected the edit workflow: the change_config endpoint previously required the API key to be present and non-empty on every save, forcing the key to round-trip through the client. The browser JavaScript stored the key in a reactive state object and updated the in-memory tool list with the credential value, further increasing the window of exposure in client-side memory and network traffic.

Affected component: the website sub-application of MISP Modules, specifically the external_tools module (serializer in models.py, list endpoint, and the external_tools_index.html template). The impact is limited to confidentiality of the stored API keys; no integrity or availability impact on the MISP Modules website itself is indicated by the patch.

An unauthenticated client could trigger this by sending a crafted XML request to a server built with Guththila, the default parser, causing the request to be parsed incorrectly or, in some cases, the process to crash. advisories.summary: The MISP Modules website component exposes external tool management endpoints (add, delete,...
advisories.description: The MISP Modules website component exposes external tool management endpoints (add, delete, change status, and change configuration) that did not enforce the optional administrator authentication policy. When ADMIN_PASSWORD was configured in the application environment, the module configuration endpoints correctly required an authenticated administrator session, but the external tools management handlers processed requests from anonymous users without any authorization check. An unauthenticated attacker with network access to the website could add arbitrary external tools, delete existing tools, toggle their active status, and modify their configurations including API keys and ingestion URLs. This inconsistency allowed bypass of the intended access control for the external tools management functionality. The vulnerability is conditional on ADMIN_PASSWORD being set; installations without an admin password intentionally permit open management access by design. The affected component is the external_tools Flask blueprint within the MISP Modules website application.

advisories.summary: A link-following flaw was found in the authorized_key module of the ansible.posix collection,...
advisories.description: A link-following flaw was found in the authorized_key module of the ansible.posix collection, residual to the fix for CVE-2026-11837. That fix guards only the final path component (os.chown with follow_symlinks=False and O_NOFOLLOW in _safe_open_write()). When an unprivileged local user replaces their ~/.ssh directory with a symlink to a directory they do not own, and an operator subsequently runs the authorized_key task as root (a common provisioning pattern), the module resolves its path operations through the symlink: atomic_move() writes the temporary file in the symlink target and renames it to <target>/authorized_keys, creating or overwriting a file in the attacker-chosen directory, and os.chmod(sshdir, 0o700) follows the symlink and changes the target directory's permissions. The written file is chowned to the unprivileged user, so this is not a privilege escalation, but it allows an attacker to create or overwrite files (for example in /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/, which APT reads regardless of file ownership) to cause integrity and availability impacts.

advisories.summary: A cleartext storage flaw was found in the AAP Gateway Operator. When reconciling an...
advisories.description: A cleartext storage flaw was found in the AAP Gateway Operator. When reconciling an AutomationController, the operator reads the protected resource-server Secret (Secret/<aap-name>-resource-server, key controller_resource_server_secret) and copies its plaintext value into the generated AutomationController custom resource under spec.extra_settings (RESOURCE_SERVER.SECRET_KEY). Although the operator uses no_log to keep the value out of its own logs, serializing it into the custom resource exposes it to any principal able to read the AutomationController CR without permission to read the backing Kubernetes Secret, breaking the expected OpenShift RBAC separation between the two resources. The value may also propagate into Kubernetes API/etcd storage, GitOps and Argo diffs and history, rendered manifests, support bundles, and audit data. The resource-server secret is intended for trusted Gateway-to-Controller service authentication, and its disclosure may allow a user to impersonate a trusted Controller service and reach privileged service-index APIs.

advisories.summary:
A flaw was found in GDB's STABS debug format parser. The
read_member_functions() function in gdb...
advisories.description:
A flaw was found in GDB's STABS debug format parser. The
read_member_functions() function in gdb/stabsread.c contains a linked
list removal bug in the code that separates destructor and non-destructor
member functions of C++ classes. The bug causes the destructor entries to
remain in the main function list while the list length counter is
decremented, resulting in an out-of-bounds write when the function list
is copied to its final allocated array. An attacker can craft an ELF
binary with malicious .stab and .stabstr sections that triggers this
out-of-bounds write when a user opens the file in GDB and performs any
symbol-inspection operation such as setting a breakpoint. The inferior
process does not need to be executed. Under controlled conditions, this
was demonstrated to achieve execution of arbitrary commands within the
GDB process.

advisories.summary: A flaw was found in the libblkid library of util-linux. During nested partition probing, the BSD,...
advisories.description: A flaw was found in the libblkid library of util-linux. During nested partition probing, the BSD, Minix, Solaris x86, and UnixWare partition probers cache a raw pointer to a parent partition entry in a dynamically allocated array. When subsequent partition additions cause the array to be reallocated, this pointer becomes stale, leading to a heap use-after-free read. An attacker who can present a crafted block device image (for example, via USB insertion or a loop-mounted disk image) can trigger this flaw without user interaction, as libblkid is invoked automatically by udev/udisks as root on block-device hot-plug events. This could lead to limited information disclosure or denial of service.

advisories.summary: An incorrect authorization flaw was found in AWX, the automation controller component of Red Hat...
advisories.description: An incorrect authorization flaw was found in AWX, the automation controller component of Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform. The API access classes for JobTemplate and WorkflowJobTemplate do not check the caller's Credential use_role when assigning the single-valued webhook_credential foreign key: JobTemplateAccess.can_add/can_change and WorkflowJobTemplateAccess.can_change in awx/main/access.py omit the check_related('webhook_credential', Credential, ..., role_field='use_role') call that UnifiedCredentialsMixin.can_attach performs for the normal many-to-many credentials relationship, and the serializer validates only the credential's type and namespace. A user who may administer their own job template (or workflow job template) and use its project and inventory can therefore attach a webhook token credential (for example a GitLab token) that they do not have use permission on. The template administrator can retrieve the template's webhook key; a subsequent webhook event causes AWX to decrypt the attached token and send it in the request header (for GitLab, PRIVATE-TOKEN) to a status URL derived from the event payload, disclosing the victim's token to a destination the attacker can influence. This may disclose another user's personal access token and allow whatever actions that token permits.

advisories.summary: The Wikidata Lookup expansion module (wiki.py) in MISP misp-modules contained a SPARQL injection...
advisories.description: The Wikidata Lookup expansion module (wiki.py) in MISP misp-modules contained a SPARQL injection vulnerability. The handler function constructed a SPARQL query by directly concatenating the user-supplied text value into the query string without any escaping or parameterization: 'SELECT ?item WHERE { ?item rdfs:label"' + request.get("text") + '" @en }'. An authenticated MISP user with access to the module could supply a crafted text attribute value containing SPARQL syntax (quotes, closing braces, UNION, SERVICE, LIMIT, etc.) to alter the structure of the query sent to the Wikidata SPARQL endpoint. This could allow an attacker to modify the query logic, extract unintended data, or cause the query to fail in ways that expose internal error details. Additionally, the old error handling path formatted raw exception objects into the response string ('wikidata API not accessible {}'.format(e)), potentially leaking internal information such as proxy credentials, query contents, or response bodies. The module also used a spoofed browser user-agent string and the deprecated Wikidata endpoint. The vulnerability required authenticated access to the MISP instance and the ability to invoke the wiki expansion module with a text attribute. The impact is limited to manipulation of the enrichment query and potential disclosure of internal error details; it does not directly compromise the MISP server or its stored data.

advisories.description: A flaw was found in GStreamer's adaptive streaming demuxers (HLS, DASH, MSS). When processing a media playlist or manifest, URIs referenced in the manifest content are fetched without restricting which URI schemes are permitted. An attacker who controls a manifest URL, or who can inject content into an HTTP manifest response, can include file:// URIs pointing to arbitrary local files, causing the affected application to read and process those files. In automated or server-side deployments such as media recorders, proxies, and downloaders, this can lead to disclosure of sensitive local files. Existence of files can also be inferred through differing error responses even when content is not directly observable.

advisories.summary: In OpenStack Aodh before 22.0.1, the alarm list API bypasses project scoping when the...
advisories.description: In OpenStack Aodh before 22.0.1, the alarm list API bypasses project scoping when the all_projects query parameter is set to false. The API checks for the presence of the all_projects key rather than its value; a true value enforces the administrator-only policy, but a false value removes the key and skips the branch that normally restricts results to the caller's project. A non-admin user with the reader role can list alarms from all projects, exposing alarm actions containing trust webhook URLs, Heat signal endpoints, project IDs, and user IDs. The parameter can also be combined with a foreign project_id to target a specific project's alarms. A related concern is that OpenStack Watcher does not apply authorization to its webhook trigger endpoint. Any authenticated user who learns an audit's webhook URL, for example from this leaked Aodh alarm metadata, can start an EVENT audit and its associated action plan regardless of their own project or role. The webhook endpoint has lacked policy enforcement since its introduction in the Ussuri release (Watcher 4.0.0).

advisories.summary: Data::Dump::Streamer versions before 3.00 for Perl allow code injection via unescaped Regexp...
advisories.description:
Data::Dump::Streamer versions before 3.00 for Perl allow code injection via unescaped Regexp patterns in _dump_qr.

A Regexp's pattern is written into a qr literal without escaping "$" or "@", so "@{[ ... ]}" and "${\ ... }" in the pattern run as code when the dump is evaluated. An already escaped delimiter gets a second backslash, which leaves the delimiter bare and ends the qr literal early.

An attacker who supplies a pattern that an application compiles, dumps and later restores with eval or do can run arbitrary Perl code.

Consequently, the utility can create files in arbitrary locations with the permissions of the executing user.

advisories.summary: A use-after-free flaw was found in mutter in the Wayland color-management ICC image-description...
advisories.description: A use-after-free flaw was found in mutter in the Wayland color-management ICC image-description path. A local attacker who can run a malicious Wayland client can destroy a wp_image_description_v1 resource while an asynchronous ICC file read is still in progress. When the read completes, the compositor uses the freed wl_resource, writes into freed memory, and frees a pointer derived from that memory. This can crash the GNOME session and may allow arbitrary code execution within the compositor process.

advisories.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: fix potencial OOB in...
advisories.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: fix potencial OOB in get_file_all_info() for compound requests

When a compound request consists of QUERY_DIRECTORY + QUERY_INFO
(FILE_ALL_INFORMATION) and the first command consumes nearly the entire
max_trans_size, get_file_all_info() would blindly call smbConvertToUTF16()
with PATH_MAX, causing out-of-bounds write beyond the response buffer.
In get_file_all_info(), there was a missing validation check for
the client-provided OutputBufferLength before copying the filename into
FileName field of the smb2_file_all_info structure.
If the filename length exceeds the available buffer space, it could lead to
potential buffer overflows or memory corruption during smbConvertToUTF16
conversion. This calculating the actual free buffer size using
smb2_calc_max_out_buf_len() and returning -EINVAL if the buffer is
insufficient and updating smbConvertToUTF16 to use the actual filename
length (clamped by PATH_MAX) to ensure a safe copy operation.

advisories.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sched/mmcid: Prevent CID...
advisories.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sched/mmcid: Prevent CID stalls due to concurrent forks

A newly forked task is accounted as MMCID user before the task is visible
in the process' thread list and the global task list. This creates the
following problem:

 CPU1			CPU2
 fork()
   sched_mm_cid_fork(tnew1)
     tnew1->mm.mm_cid_users++;
     tnew1->mm_cid.cid = getcid()
-> preemption
			fork()
			  sched_mm_cid_fork(tnew2)
			    tnew2->mm.mm_cid_users++;
                            // Reaches the per CPU threshold
			    mm_cid_fixup_tasks_to_cpus()
			    for_each_other(current, p)
			         ....

As tnew1 is not visible yet, this fails to fix up the already allocated CID
of tnew1. As a consequence a subsequent schedule in might fail to acquire a
(transitional) CID and the machine stalls.

Move the invocation of sched_mm_cid_fork() after the new task becomes
visible in the thread and the task list to prevent this.

This also makes it symmetrical vs. exit() where the task is removed as CID
user before the task is removed from the thread and task lists.

advisories.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

rust_binder: fix oneway spam...
advisories.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

rust_binder: fix oneway spam detection

The spam detection logic in TreeRange was executed before the current
request was inserted into the tree. So the new request was not being
factored in the spam calculation. Fix this by moving the logic after
the new range has been inserted.

Also, the detection logic for ArrayRange was missing altogether which
meant large spamming transactions could get away without being detected.
Fix this by implementing an equivalent low_oneway_space() in ArrayRange.

Note that I looked into centralizing this logic in RangeAllocator but
iterating through 'state' and 'size' got a bit too complicated (for me)
and I abandoned this effort.

advisories.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

rust_binder: avoid reading...
advisories.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

rust_binder: avoid reading the written value in offsets array

When sending a transaction, its offsets array is first copied into the
target proc's vma, and then the values are read back from there. This is
normally fine because the vma is a read-only mapping, so the target
process cannot change the value under us.

However, if the target process somehow gains the ability to write to its
own vma, it could change the offset before it's read back, causing the
kernel to misinterpret what the sender meant. If the sender happens to
send a payload with a specific shape, this could in the worst case lead
to the receiver being able to privilege escalate into the sender.

The intent is that gaining the ability to change the read-only vma of
your own process should not be exploitable, so remove this TOCTOU read
even though it's unexploitable without another Binder bug.

advisories.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sched/mmcid: Handle vfork()...
advisories.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sched/mmcid: Handle vfork()/CLONE_VM correctly

Matthieu and Jiri reported stalls where a task endlessly loops in
mm_get_cid() when scheduling in.

It turned out that the logic which handles vfork()'ed tasks is broken. It
is invoked when the number of tasks associated to a process is smaller than
the number of MMCID users. It then walks the task list to find the
vfork()'ed task, but accounts all the already processed tasks as well.

If that double processing brings the number of to be handled tasks to 0,
the walk stops and the vfork()'ed task's CID is not fixed up. As a
consequence a subsequent schedule in fails to acquire a (transitional) CID
and the machine stalls.

Cure this by removing the accounting condition and make the fixup always
walk the full task list if it could not find the exact number of users in
the process' thread list.

advisories.summary: A re-entrancy flaw in Node.js HTTPS lets an unauthenticated client read memory belonging to other...
advisories.description: A re-entrancy flaw in Node.js HTTPS lets an unauthenticated client read memory belonging to other connections, including TLS private keys and other users' requests. TLSWrap::DoWrite() calls ClearOut() directly when asked to write zero bytes; if that write is issued from JavaScript running inside the HTTP parser's on_body callback, ClearOut() decrypts the next TLS record while the parser is still mid-body, re-entering llhttp_execute() and causing a use-after-free and an out-of-bounds heap read. The server then copies that freed or unrelated heap memory into the response for the request body. Triggering it requires a handler that calls res.flushHeaders() before the request body ends and later calls res.end() with a non-empty chunk, and reading the leaked memory requires any ordinary route that echoes or stores a request body. Cleartext node:http is not affected. This vulnerability affects Node.js 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x.

advisories.summary: A per-host mutual-TLS authorization bypass in Node.js lets a client authorized for the default...
advisories.description: A per-host mutual-TLS authorization bypass in Node.js lets a client authorized for the default hostname reach a protected hostname it is not authorized for. When a TLS server assigns a hostname a different client-certificate CA with server.addContext(host, { ca: protectedCA }) but no server certificate in that SNI context, the per-host client CA is never installed and the handshake falls back to the default client CA. In src/crypto/crypto_tls.cc, CertCbDone installs the SNI context's CA only when setSniContext succeeds, but setSniContext returns false for a context with no server certificate, so a CA-only SNI context silently keeps the default CA. A client holding a certificate trusted by the default CA, but not the protected CA, can therefore complete mTLS to the protected hostname and read its response even with requestCert and rejectUnauthorized enabled, while a client certified by the protected CA is rejected. This vulnerability affects Node.js 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x.

advisories.summary: A client certificate authentication bypass in Node.js TLS lets a client change the servername...

advisories.summary: A reachable assertion in Node.js HTTP/2 session teardown lets any unauthenticated client abort...
advisories.description: A reachable assertion in Node.js HTTP/2 session teardown lets any unauthenticated client abort the server, over both TLS and cleartext. A client can arrange for an Http2Stream that still holds nghttp2-allocated header buffers to outlive its session: the stream is removed from the session's stream set but never detached, so when ~Http2Session() runs the memory accounting is nonzero and the CHECK_EQ(current_nghttp2_memory_, 0) assertion fails, terminating the process. The trigger needs only a default http2 server whose handler responds before the request body has ended, which is typical. It is a variant of CVE-2024-27983 that the earlier fix did not cover, because that fix only detached streams still tracked in the session. This vulnerability affects Node.js 26.x (since 26.9.0) and 24.x (since 24.22.0).

advisories.summary: A use-after-free in Node.js HTTP/2 lets an unauthenticated client corrupt server memory, over...
advisories.description: A use-after-free in Node.js HTTP/2 lets an unauthenticated client corrupt server memory, over both TLS and cleartext, when the server serves files with respondWithFile() or respondWithFD(). A client can make the server free an Http2Stream while a write request that points to it is still queued on the socket; when that write completes, the code dereferences and makes a virtual call through the freed object. The only precondition is that the application serves a file with stream.respondWithFile() or stream.respondWithFD(), with default settings otherwise. This vulnerability affects Node.js 26.x (since 26.9.0) and 24.x (since 24.22.0).

advisories.summary: Node.js discloses proxy credentials in ERR_PROXY_INVALID_CONFIG error messages. CVE-2026-48615...
advisories.description: Node.js discloses proxy credentials in ERR_PROXY_INVALID_CONFIG error messages. CVE-2026-48615 established that a proxy credential must not appear in a Node.js error message and redacted the username and password from ProxyConfig.href, but that fix missed four error paths in the same subsystem, one of them inside the same constructor, which interpolate the raw proxy URL, credentials included, into an ERR_PROXY_INVALID_CONFIG message. The proxy URL comes from the environment, but the defect is the sink: a secret that Node.js redacts everywhere else is emitted verbatim into a much wider audience than the process environment, such as stderr, container logs, log aggregation, and crash reporting services. This vulnerability affects Node.js 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x.

advisories.summary: An unauthenticated HTTP/2 client can permanently leak Node.js server memory and file descriptors....
advisories.description: An unauthenticated HTTP/2 client can permanently leak Node.js server memory and file descriptors. If a peer triggers a protocol error, for example an oversized frame header, while the session is already shutting down, nghttp2 tears the session down internally but Node.js never notices, leaving a dangling session: the socket stays in CLOSE_WAIT and all of Node.js's HTTP/2 state for that connection is held in memory indefinitely, with no further cost to the attacker. The attacker can start the shutdown remotely by sending GOAWAY(NO_ERROR), so it is reliable against default HTTP/2 servers. It is an incomplete-fix case of CVE-2026-48937: that fix detected nghttp2 internal terminations by watching for GOAWAY sent while not shutting down, but missed terminations that arrive while the session is already shutting down. This vulnerability affects Node.js 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x.

advisories.summary: An uncatchable exception in the Node.js zlib streaming API lets a peer crash a process by...
advisories.description: An uncatchable exception in the Node.js zlib streaming API lets a peer crash a process by disconnecting while data is being compressed. zlib.params() queues a flush and completes its work in that write's callback; if the stream is destroyed first, as pipeline() does when the peer goes away, Writable still invokes the callback with an error, but the callback ignores its arguments and asserts that the native handle still exists. The handle is gone, so an ERR_INTERNAL_ASSERTION is thrown from inside stream internals and bypasses the stream's error event, the params() callback, and the pipeline() callback, terminating the process. An application is affected only if it calls deflate.params() while streaming to a peer, which is uncommon. This vulnerability affects Node.js 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x.

advisories.summary: A certificate validation bypass in Node.js https.Agent lets a cached TLS session authenticated...
advisories.description: A certificate validation bypass in Node.js https.Agent lets a cached TLS session authenticated under one CA policy be reused by a later request with a stricter policy. https.Agent.prototype.getName() assigns the same Agent and session-cache key to a request that omits ca and one that explicitly supplies ca: [], because an omitted value appends nothing to the key while an empty array stringifies to an empty string. The two policies differ: omitting ca uses the default trust store, while supplying ca replaces it. Since they share a key, a TLS session authenticated under the broader default policy is handed to a new connection made under the later ca: [] policy, and TLS 1.3 session resumption carries the earlier authentication forward, so the second request reports authorized === true and transmits confidential data to a server its own CA policy would reject on a fresh connection. This vulnerability affects Node.js 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x.

advisories.summary: A one-byte heap buffer overflow in Node.js HTTP/2 Alt-Svc handling lets a remote, unauthenticated...
advisories.description: A one-byte heap buffer overflow in Node.js HTTP/2 Alt-Svc handling lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker corrupt process memory. When an application passes an attacker-controlled value such as a request's :authority header to Http2Session.altsvc(), the AltSvc implementation in src/node_http2.cc allocates a buffer sized to the origin length and then writes it with a null terminator, placing one byte past the end of the allocation. A single request carrying a long but syntactically valid :authority triggers the out-of-bounds write, which aborts the process and serves as a remote heap-corruption primitive. This vulnerability affects Node.js 26.x and 24.x.

advisories.summary: A deferred-callback use-after-destroy in Node.js TLS server handshake handling allows a remote,...
advisories.description: A deferred-callback use-after-destroy in Node.js TLS server handshake handling allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to terminate the server process. When a TLS server uses any of the SNICallback, OCSPRequest, newSession, or resumeSession hooks, or server.addContext(), the corresponding OpenSSL callbacks are deferred, and the deferred code does not handle the underlying socket being destroyed between scheduling and execution. By sending a client hello that reaches the vulnerable path (for example, no SNI together with an OCSP request) followed by padding and a socket FIN, an attacker makes OpenSSL deliver the client hello and the end-of-file in the same tick, so the socket is destroyed before the deferred callback runs and the process raises an uncaught exception instead of emitting an 'error' event. This vulnerability affects Node.js 26.x and 24.x.

advisories.summary: A NULL pointer dereference in Node.js HTTP/2 lets an unauthenticated client crash the server,...
advisories.description: A NULL pointer dereference in Node.js HTTP/2 lets an unauthenticated client crash the server, over both TLS and cleartext, by cancelling file downloads. When the server serves a file with stream.respondWithFile() or stream.respondWithFD() and the client cancels the request, a StreamPipe used for the transfer is torn down in an order that leaves a NULL pointer which is then dereferenced, aborting the process. No crafted frames are needed, and a handful of cancelled requests against a default file-serving handler is enough. This vulnerability affects Node.js 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x.

advisories.summary: A Permission Model bypass in Node.js recursive file watching discloses the names of files and...
advisories.description: A Permission Model bypass in Node.js recursive file watching discloses the names of files and directories the process is not permitted to read. On macOS and Windows, fs.watch() and fs.promises.watch() in recursive mode are backed by the native libuv watcher: FSEventWrap::Start checks kFileSystemRead only once, on the watched root, and FSEventWrap::OnEvent then forwards every filename libuv reports (relative paths at any depth) to the JavaScript callback without checking that each path is covered by the read grant. Code running under --permission with an exact read grant on a directory can therefore learn names such as sub/secret.txt even though readdir on that subdirectory is denied. The flaw exposes names and timing metadata, not file contents, and requires macOS or Windows plus files created under the watched directory by another actor. This vulnerability affects Node.js 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

advisories.summary: An unauthenticated HTTP/2 client can exhaust Node.js server memory because inbound DATA queued on...
advisories.description: An unauthenticated HTTP/2 client can exhaust Node.js server memory because inbound DATA queued on an undrained stream is charged to no session budget. Each inbound DATA frame creates one JavaScript Buffer view in the receiving stream's readable queue, but nothing charges that queue to current_session_memory_: the socket read buffer is accounted only during parsing and released immediately, so whatever stays queued is accounted to nothing. A peer that fills a stream's receive window with one-byte DATA frames pays about 10 wire bytes per frame while the server retains about 114 bytes per frame, so a single stream on one connection can retain hundreds of megabytes from tens of megabytes sent. maxSessionMemory neither bounds the growth nor refuses new streams, because Http2Session::CanAddStream gates admission on the same counter that never sees the queue. This vulnerability affects Node.js 26.x and 24.x.

advisories.summary: A use-after-free in Node.js HTTP/2 stream teardown can leak response memory, including the...
advisories.description: A use-after-free in Node.js HTTP/2 stream teardown can leak response memory, including the contents of other connections' response buffers, to a peer. When a stream is torn down while a write is still backpressured, for example by a peer RST_STREAM or by the server's own per-stream timeout destroying the stream, the stream's response buffer is freed but a reference to it is still used, so freed or unrelated heap memory is written to the socket instead of the intended response. On Node.js 26.x and 24.x the teardown can be driven purely by a remote peer once the window-size change from 26.9.0 and 24.22.0 is present, and on all supported lines the same defect is reachable through an application-initiated teardown such as a per-stream idle timeout. This vulnerability affects Node.js 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x.

advisories.summary: repmgr 4.0.0 through 5.5.0 is affected by an OS command injection vulnerability (CWE-78) in event...
advisories.description: repmgr 4.0.0 through 5.5.0 is affected by an OS command injection vulnerability (CWE-78) in event notifications. When event_notification_command is configured, repmgr substitutes the %a (node name), %c (connection string) and %d (details) placeholders into the command and runs it through the shell. %a and %c are inserted without escaping, and %d escapes only double quotes, so shell command substitution still works inside the quoting the documentation recommends. The node name and connection string come from node records in the repmgr.nodes table. An attacker with the credentials of a non-superuser repmgr database user can write a crafted node record and run OS commands, as the operating system user that runs repmgr or repmgrd (usually postgres), on other cluster nodes that process an event using these placeholders. The %a placeholder of failover_validation_command has the same flaw. Deployments whose repmgr database user is a superuser gain no new capability, because a superuser can already run OS commands, and deployments that do not use these placeholders are not affected. The issue is fixed in repmgr 5.5.1. After upgrading, operators must remove any quotes they placed around these placeholders, because a placeholder left inside double quotes is still open to command injection.

advisories.summary: In proxygen's HTTP/3 session, when a HEADERS block referenced QPACK dynamic table entries that...
advisories.description: In proxygen's HTTP/3 session, when a HEADERS block referenced QPACK dynamic table entries that had not yet been received, header decoding for that stream was paused, but the session continued to read the stream from the QUIC transport. The unread data bypassed the session's ingress buffer limit, returned flow-control credit to the peer, and was re-scanned in full on every read. With QPACK blocked streams enabled (the default), a remote, unauthenticated HTTP/3 peer could send a HEADERS block that references a dynamic table insert it never sends, followed by a continuous stream of data, causing memory growth until the request timed out and CPU usage that grows quadratically, leading to denial of service. advisories.summary: The regcomp and regexec functions in the GNU C Library version 2.3 to version 2.44 may read freed...
advisories.description:
The regcomp and regexec functions in the GNU C Library version 2.3 to version 2.44 may read freed memory and free the same heap block twice when a memory allocation fails while a regular expression is compiled or matched.  The re_dfa_add_node (the NFA node table) and build_range_exp (bracket ranges) grow several arrays with consecutive realloc calls and store the new pointers only after all of them succeed.  When a later call fails, the pattern buffer keeps pointers to blocks that were already freed, and the error cleanup frees them again.  In regexec, the back-reference cache (match_ctx_add_entry) frees its array when a realloc fails but keeps the pointer, which is freed again on the error path.

An attacker does not need to supply a crafted regular expression: patterns large enough to grow these arrays are common.  The failure has to hit a specific allocation, though, so the issue can only be reached when the system is already under memory pressure.  An attacker who supplies the pattern or the subject string has little control over which allocation fails, so the expected impact is a crash of the process.  This issue affects all architectures and ABIs supported by the GNU C Library.

advisories.summary: Calling the wide scanf family of functions (swscanf, fwscanf, wscanf, vswscanf, vfwscanf and...
advisories.description:
Calling the wide scanf family of functions (swscanf, fwscanf, wscanf, vswscanf, vfwscanf and vwscanf) with a %s or %[ conversion without the 'l' length modifier in the GNU C Library version 2.2 to version 2.44 writes an extra null byte one past the end of the destination array when the converted multibyte string and its terminating null byte exactly fill that array.

These conversions store each wide input character into the caller's char array as a multibyte sequence.  The conversion ends with the sequence that returns to the initial shift state, which also stores the terminating null byte, and the functions then append a second null byte.  A destination sized for the converted string and one terminator, as the C standard requires the caller to provide, is therefore written one byte past its end.  The out-of-bounds byte is always a null byte, which may corrupt adjacent data or crash the process.  An attacker who supplies the input can trigger the overflow with a string whose converted length exactly fills the destination.

The narrow scanf functions, the %ls and %l[ conversions into a wchar_t array, and the 'a' and 'm' allocation modifiers are not affected, and storing a wide scanf conversion into a narrow char array is uncommon.  This issue affects all architectures and ABIs supported by the GNU C Library.

advisories.summary: The WPML Multilingual CMS plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Authentication Bypass via Race...
advisories.description: The WPML Multilingual CMS plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Authentication Bypass via Race Condition in versions up to, and including, 4.9.7. This is due to the `process_iframe_request` function's language-per-domain SSO handler generating the cross-domain sign-in token via `wp_create_nonce('wpml_sso')` on the logout landing page, where the browser has already discarded its authentication cookies — so `wp_get_session_token()` returns an empty string and the token collapses to the shared anonymous nonce for the current 12-hour tick rather than a user-bound secret — and then storing it in the `wpml_sso_user_<token>_<sha256('wpml_sso'.$domain)>` transient mapped to the victim's `user_id` with no binding to the specific sign-out action or requesting client. Because an unauthenticated attacker can independently derive the identical token by triggering the logout confirmation flow on `wp-login.php?action=logout`, and because the `is_iframe_request()` gate conditions (the per-domain SSO `started` transient and domain-hash derived from the public constant `SSO_NONCE`) are fully computable within the 60-second `SSO_TIMEOUT` window, an unauthenticated attacker can submit the forged `wpml_sso_token_domain` parameter with a `wpml_user_signed_in` status to a secondary language-domain endpoint before the legitimate `wpml_user_signed_out` iframe fires, causing WordPress authentication cookies to be issued for the victim. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to gain access to accounts of users — including administrators — who are actively in the process of logging out during the race window.

advisories.summary: The Ninja Forms - File Uploads add-on for WordPress is vulnerable to Arbitrary File Deletion (and...
advisories.description: The Ninja Forms - File Uploads add-on for WordPress is vulnerable to Arbitrary File Deletion (and arbitrary file read via S3/Dropbox/Google Drive exfiltration) in versions up to, and including, 3.3.36. The flaw spans NF_FU_Fields_Upload::process() in includes/fields/upload.php — which returns early (leaving the client-supplied files[] intact) whenever a public submission carries a nonempty extra.saveProgress — and NF_FU_External_Abstracts_Service::process_upload() in includes/external/abstracts/service.php, whose authoritative-path reload only fires when the client sends upload_id. By omitting upload_id, an attacker's data[file_path] survives into the Background Upload queue and is used by both upload_file_to_s3() (as SourceFile) and the maybe_delete_server_file() unlink() call in includes/external/abstracts/backgroundupload.php, with no canonicalization or upload-directory containment check (the plugin's own is_path_within_upload_dir() helper is only applied on admin paths). This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to delete arbitrary files on the affected site's server which may make remote code execution possible — specifically, deleting wp-config.php forces WordPress into its setup screen, enabling full site takeover.

Roller treats weblog administrators as untrusted and exposes weblog and entry data to templates only through wrapper classes, but a public accessor on those wrapper classes returned the underlying persistent object directly, including the stored password hash of the weblog's creator and of any author whose entry renders on the page. advisories.summary: Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference in Apache Roller 4.0 through 6.1.6 allows...

The entry body is parsed with a parser configuration that permits external parameter entities and external DTD subsets, and the parse happens before any per-weblog authorization check and before any check of whether the AtomPub feature is enabled, so the endpoint is reachable by any authenticated account on a default installation. Users are recommended to upgrade to Apache Roller 6.1.7 or later, which parses AtomPub entries with a hardened XML configuration and rejects AtomPub requests while the feature is disabled.

advisories.summary: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) in the Planet feed aggregator administration of Apache Roller 4...
advisories.description: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) in the Planet feed aggregator administration of Apache Roller 4.0 through 6.1.6 allows an unauthenticated attacker to make the Roller server fetch a URL the attacker chooses, including internal addresses, by inducing a logged-in global administrator to open a crafted web page. The action that adds a Planet subscription can be triggered cross-site; in recent releases it accepts GET requests, which Roller's CSRF token check does not cover. The action fetches the supplied URL and saves the subscription, and any fetched content that parses as a feed is then published without authentication in the aggregated Planet feed. The Planet aggregator is enabled by default. Users are recommended to upgrade to Apache Roller 6.1.7 or later, which requires POST requests with a valid CSRF token for Planet administration changes and turns the Planet aggregator off by default.

This matters when weblog authors are not trusted with script (weblogAdminsUntrusted=true, the default since 6.1.4). AtomPub is disabled by default. Users are recommended to upgrade to Apache Roller 6.1.7 or later, which removes HTML characters from tag names, including names stored earlier.

advisories.summary: A flaw was found in the login-failure storage component of Keycloak, the identity and access...
advisories.description: A flaw was found in the login-failure storage component of Keycloak, the identity and access management solution. This issue specifically affects deployments using MySQL or MariaDB databases in a multi-node configuration. When multiple failed login attempts occur simultaneously for the same account, a synchronization error can cause the system to enter a repetitive loop that locks the user's record in the database. This results in legitimate login attempts for that user being blocked and failing with an error. Furthermore, because some failures are not correctly recorded during this loop, the system's brute-force protection may not accurately count all failed attempts.

advisories.description: A flaw was found in cockpit-files. A local unprivileged attacker can exploit a race condition during directory creation with owner assignment. By controlling a writable parent directory, the attacker can replace a newly created directory with a symbolic link (symlink) before the ownership change operation (chown) is applied. advisories.summary: A flaw was found in libsoup's WebSocket implementation when using the permessage-deflate...
advisories.description: A flaw was found in libsoup's WebSocket implementation when using the permessage-deflate extension. The extension's decompression loop (inflate()) processes data in chunks without enforcing an upper boundary limit on the output buffer size. While libsoup limits the incoming compressed frame size via max_incoming_payload_size, it fails to track or limit memory allocation during decompression. A separate check for decompressed size (max_total_message_size) exists but executes only after inflation is complete, and it is entirely disabled by default for client connections. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can exploit this by sending a small, highly compressed payload (a decompression bomb), causing unbounded memory allocation that triggers an Out-of-Memory (OOM) crash and a Denial of Service (DoS).

advisories.description: A flaw was found in BusyBox. advisories.summary: The 6Storage Rentals plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Authentication Bypass leading to...
advisories.description: The 6Storage Rentals plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Authentication Bypass leading to Administrator Account Takeover in all versions up to, and including, 2.31.0. The vulnerability exists because the `six_storage_portal_registration()` AJAX handler — registered on `wp_ajax_six_storage_portal_plugin_registration` — performs no capability check and no nonce verification before writing the caller-supplied `six_storage_online_api_url` POST parameter to the site-wide option of the same name; the unauthenticated `six_storage_create_wp_user()` handler then redeems a transient seeded from that attacker-controlled URL's response and unconditionally calls `wp_set_current_user()` and `wp_set_auth_cookie()` with no ownership or credential verification. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with Subscriber-level access and above, to authenticate as any existing WordPress user — including any administrator whose email address is known or guessable — resulting in full site compromise. This issue represents an incomplete fix for a prior vulnerability: the 2.29.0 remediation moved the target email out of POST data into a server-side transient, but because any Subscriber can still overwrite the outbound API URL that populates that transient, the full authentication bypass chain remains exploitable in three AJAX requests.

advisories.summary: A flaw was found in cockpit-files. This vulnerability allows a local attacker to exploit a timing...
advisories.description: A flaw was found in cockpit-files. This vulnerability allows a local attacker to exploit a timing issue, known as a symlink race condition, during privileged file operations such as changing file ownership or permissions. By manipulating directory entries and winning this race, the attacker can redirect these operations to unintended files. This could lead to unauthorized changes in file ownership and permissions on arbitrary files, potentially compromising system integrity and availability by altering system or application states or rendering services unusable.

advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (37b270c23bd05f704fa06ea349aefd2d956af3fdcd3a851a5a7b89bc22493a12)

advisories.summary: Malicious code in @wanzforme/bails4u (npm)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (7db6d4bfe675bbaa2043f2958993761070ab6e5a09572d884082465b51bdf437)
package.json declares a runtime dependency `libsignal` with the source `github:wanzchil/libsignal-node`. The reference has no commit SHA, tag, or integrity hash, so `npm install` resolves whatever the referenced repository's default branch currently contains and executes any lifecycle scripts bundled with it on the installer's machine. The owner of wanzchil/libsignal-node can push new commits at any time, and future installs will fetch and run those bytes with no version pin and no verification — fully bypassing the npm registry's integrity model for this dependency. advisories.summary: Malicious code in formatting-subtitles (npm)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (25577370189f57a5678b2f2c45e212abfc79a3675dc7d51581f633e78aba47a6)
package.json declares `preinstall: sh./prepare.js && exit 0`. prepare.js is shaped like JavaScript (ending with `console.log('hello world')`) but is executed by /bin/sh, which does not treat `/**... */` as a comment. Inside that block, sh evaluates two `$(...)` command substitutions: one issues a GET to the hardcoded collector https://webhook.site/9e8c8742-3102-4716-aa8b-e150e9e84fe7/stats_1, and the other downloads https://api.github.com/gists/da04f14c93acbe9a7aef827be0a2e91c, extracts a file via jq, writes it to disk as `x`, and runs it with `sh x`. On `npm install`, the installer host fetches and executes arbitrary, unpinned, attacker-controlled content from a mutable GitHub Gist, and the webhook.site beacon discloses the install (and curl-visible metadata such as public IP and user-agent) to the attacker. The JS-comment-wrapping of the shell payload is a deliberate cover story so prepare.js reads as a trivial hello-world when viewed as JavaScript.

advisories.summary: Malicious code in @securihackbot/depconf-flow-1792484611 (npm)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (6dc8c3628b1d44eca51a5cde6143c1760a5d393b45729f174bab73f76f8641e8)
Package publishes under the `@securihackbot` scope as a public dependency-confusion squat of an internal name. The declared `postinstall` script executes `postinstall.js`, which on `npm install` collects host identifiers (os.hostname(), USER/USERNAME, platform, arch, node version, package name, and a nonce), base64-encodes them, and sends them as a query parameter via plain-HTTP GET to a hardcoded bare-IP collector at http://34.143.131.27:18080/. A DNS-exfil fallback resolves NONCE-prefixed subdomains under a configured DNS suffix. The exfiltration fires automatically on install with no opt-in, and any build host whose resolver pulls this public tarball instead of an intended internal `@securihackbot/*` package will beacon host metadata to the hardcoded collector. advisories.summary: Malicious code in @testsecuiitytestme/cache-helper (npm)
advisories.description:
@testsecuiitytestme/cache-helper is the only package of the npm account testsecuiitytestme. It was created on 2026-10-27 at 12:08 UTC with npm's staged-publish placeholder 0.0.0-stage, followed by 1.0.1 (12:28 UTC), 1.0.2 (15:33 UTC) and 1.0.3 (16:24 UTC); a 1.0.0 was removed before 14:21 UTC. It describes itself as "Cache helper utilities" and has no README, repository or source code. 1.0.3 was the latest version and still live at the time of this report.

Each version runs a native addon at install time. 1.0.1 has postinstall: node -e "try{require(process.platform==='win32'?'./addon_win.node':'./addon.node')}catch(e){}". 1.0.2 and 1.0.3 depend on node-gyp-build and run it as postinstall, which loads the prebuilt addon shipped in prebuilds/linux-x64/node.napi.node or prebuilds/win32-x64/node.napi.node. 1.0.3 adds a binding.gyp with an empty sources list and an install script node-gyp rebuild, so the package looks like an ordinary native module; there is no C source in any version.

The addon (Linux ELF and Windows PE) is a loader. It checks for CI and sandbox environments (GITHUB_ACTIONS, GITLAB_CI, TRAVIS, CIRCLECI, JENKINS_URL, BUILDKITE, CODEBUILD_BUILD_ID and others, plus SANDBOX), containers (/proc/1/cgroup: docker, containerd, kubepods, podman), a debugger (TracerPid), memory and CPU count, then reads the sibling file .napi_cache, writes it to a hidden temp file and runs it in a detached process.

.napi_cache is JavaScript encoded with a single-byte XOR (0x96). It exits under CI, decodes a second layer (repeating 32-byte XOR, then brotli), locates the Bun runtime or downloads bun 1.2.18 from the official oven-sh/bun GitHub releases, writes the decoded program to the temp directory and runs it detached with Bun. This loader shape matches the second wave of the Shai-Hulud npm worm.

The Bun program is obfuscated (javascript-obfuscator string table). Its strings show credential collection for npm, GitHub, GitLab, PyPI, RubyGems, JFrog, Docker Hub and GHCR, AWS, GCP, Azure, HashiCorp Vault and Kubernetes, plus .ssh, .git-credentials, .env files, browser login databases, the macOS keychain, 1Password and Bitwarden. They also show propagation: npm publishing with provenance, PyPI and RubyGems publishing, GitHub workflow and composite-action injection, GitLab CI template changes, and writes to AI assistant configuration (.claude/settings.json hooks, .cursor rules, .mcp.json, copilot-instructions.md, CLAUDE.md). The exfiltration endpoints sit behind a further string-encoding layer that was not decoded. Analysis was static only; nothing was executed.

advisories.summary: Malicious code in fetchium (PyPI)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (01ceb360b0c2d18e31f2a2f5c370bcb652417afa9b6eca94a153f5baaaf6211a)
The package presents itself as a small collection of web/utility helpers (greet/clamp) but ships a covert loader that executes on first import. __init__.py unconditionally invokes _loader.run() inside a bare try/except so any failure is swallowed silently. _loader.py is approximately 1.9 MB of base64+zlib-encoded chunks (the _CH tuple) plus a Windows dropper harness configured with _TARGET='MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.msi', _XARGS=['/qn','/quiet','/norestart'] and _SPAWN='wmi', consistent with silent MSI installation via msiexec/WMI impersonating a Microsoft Edge update. A base64-encoded JSON configuration bundled inside the loader enumerates analysis-environment indicators to evade (sandbox/cuckoo/joe/hybrid/anyrun names; VirtualBox/VMware/QEMU/Xen/Parallels process and registry fingerprints; debugging and monitoring tools such as wireshark, procmon, ida64, x64dbg; VM MAC OUI prefixes) and specifies Windows persistence under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run with subkey Microsoft\CoreRuntime. The advertised functionality bears no relationship to this payload, the loader is undisclosed in the README, and the metadata uses placeholder values. Importing the package on a Windows host triggers decoding and execution of the opaque payload, drop/execution of an MSI masquerading as a Microsoft update, and installation of a Run-key persistence entry.

## Source: amazon-inspector (83716a1c499cecbd64fe45f5ff56ab70ea6d1543e922c55e0514f2e2a69fe391)
The crate ships two reachable async payloads — `pub async fn dat` in src/test.rs and `pub async fn bs` in src/parse.rs, both imported from src/lib.rs — that walk the user's home directory with walkdir, build a zip archive via zip::ZipWriter including wallet artefacts (e.g. `exodus.wallet`), and upload the archive via reqwest multipart to a hardcoded Telegram Bot API endpoint using embedded `API_` token and `chat_id` constants. Both payload files (parse.rs ~40KB, test.rs ~60KB) are padded with roughly a hundred nonsense filler functions with invented identifiers (Modemir65, mix_wisp_30, Flagzelk147, shuffle_zelkvak_73, etc.) surrounding the exfiltration functions at the end of each file, consistent with deliberate camouflage. The dependency set — evdev and rdev (keyboard capture), winreg plus winapi winuser/processthreadsapi/memoryapi (Windows registry and process/memory primitives), walkdir, zip, and reqwest with the multipart feature — extends the capability surface to cross-platform keylogging and Windows persistence. The crate description `Это учебный проект для тестирования кибербезопасности` ("educational project for cybersecurity testing") does not match the shipped behavior.

advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (f82b1f071f557e9f25cfce6d7643f19053c6a2bd7d61470fcf114ac53e950c63)
basek 0.1.0 is a Windows keylogger shipped as a Rust library. The exposed get_data() routine polls Windows key states for alphanumeric, function, and special keys and batches captured keystrokes together with the local username. The batches are POSTed to the Telegram Bot API at api.telegram.org/bot<token>/sendMessage using a bot token stored as a byte array XORed with 0xAA and reassembled at runtime via the ut! macro, with hardcoded chat_id 7304091279; a secondary exfiltration endpoint https://keylogger.nullsect0r.tech/log is also configured. The crate installs itself for persistence: ensure_installed() copies the host binary to %LOCALAPPDATA%\WindowsSystemUtility\WinSysUtils.exe, writes an HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run value named 'WinSysUtils' for boot persistence, spawns a watchdog clone under a random 12-digit filename to respawn the keylogger, and schedules a cmd.exe timeout+del sequence to self-delete the original. A 30-second initial sleep, a 20-second warmup during which keystrokes are observed but not logged, and randomized polling jitter are used to evade sandbox and behavioral analysis. The crate description's 'educational cybersecurity project' framing is contradicted by the XOR-obfuscated exfiltration destination, hardcoded attacker chat_id, Run-key persistence, watchdog respawn, and self-delete logic.

---

advisories.summary: Malicious code in cheesebox (RubyGems)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (5b03698e5384db9f041d0e2caa51db10abc0d0dcbfc1e5e77b795acc4d8cec76)
The gem declares mkrf_conf.rb as a native extension in its gemspec, causing it to execute automatically during `gem install`. On execution the script reads installer-side system files (/etc/passwd, /etc/hosts, /etc/resolv.conf) and collects host identifiers (hostname, username, home directory, current working directory), then opens a TLS TCPSocket to the hardcoded Burp Collaborator subdomain xwx31i3e80kbj4h1s7wnh8yklbrdf33s.oastify.com on port 443 and POSTs the collected data as JSON. The destination is an attacker-controlled out-of-band interaction host, not any infrastructure related to the gem's declared purpose, and the data read is unrelated to building a native extension (no mkmf probing, no compilation of shipped sources).

---

Credit: [OpenSSF](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages) ([source](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages/blob/d96303ea4f55739f99519c744c2cd893c10b2d04/osv/malicious/rubygems/cheesebox/MAL-2026-19157.json))

advisories.summary: Malicious code in buffer-code-exercise-api (RubyGems)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (b575cb1f6c5f576af68398e3ad383942d6ec5f065456948bc51df018e7e0ab68)
The gem declares ext/mkrf_conf.rb as a native extension via the gemspec `extensions:` entry, which causes RubyGems to execute the script during `gem install`. The script performs no native build work and ships no native sources. Instead, it collects hostname, login name, current working directory, home directory, and the contents of /etc/passwd, /etc/hosts, and /etc/resolv.conf, JSON-encodes them, and POSTs them over TLS to the hardcoded host 0ef6jllhq32e17z4aaeqzbgn3e9fx5lu.oastify.com (a Burp Collaborator out-of-band interaction subdomain), preceded by a DNS probe to the same host. The destination is not associated with the package's publisher, and the files read bear no relation to building a native extension. The extension entry is used purely as an install-time execution vector.

---

Credit: [OpenSSF](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages) ([source](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages/blob/d96303ea4f55739f99519c744c2cd893c10b2d04/osv/malicious/rubygems/buffer-code-exercise-api/MAL-2026-19156.json))

advisories.summary: Malicious code in privacypass-py (PyPI)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (0ca6e88317dac5ec524d2dc6ec4b2af7934e2213569ed7c8a757e59edb45b0c3)
The package presents itself as 'Privacy Pass client primitives' but ships no cryptographic functionality. Its only runtime effect is a data-exfiltration beacon. setup.py invokes a `_report()` routine during build/install that collects hostname, username, current working directory, argv, the parent process command line read from /proc/<ppid>/cmdline, and environment variable names and values matching credential-related prefixes (AWS_, GITHUB_, PIP_, and others), then POSTs the JSON payload to the hardcoded bare-IP endpoint http://85.190.112.236:8881/b/<nonce> over plain HTTP. privacypass_py/__init__.py repeats the same beacon at module top level, calling `_report('import')` on every `import privacypass_py` with an expanded prefix list (CLOUDFLARE_, SUPERTOKENS, HOME, USER, PATH) and an additional `secretish_names` list filtered by substrings KEY/SECRET/TOKEN/PASS/CRED/PRIVATE/SEED/MNEMONIC/SIGNATURE/COOKIE/SESSION/AUTH, sent to http://85.190.112.236:8881/f/<nonce>. The import-time path fires outside pip build isolation. The name and description function as cover for a package whose only shipped code is the beacon.

---

Credit: [OpenSSF](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages) ([source](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages/blob/2803af2aa0daf7e4fd833385a7509baa41ec0757/osv/malicious/pypi/privacypass-py/MAL-2026-18435.json))

advisories.summary: Malicious code in @rfewqa-fes/mnm-doc-mcp (npm)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (0495a09022e152fe8c13b9251497c56e333b58af6e54c412bfd43ff4503be1a7)
package.json declares the sole dependency 'node-health-utils' as an off-registry HTTP tarball URL at a bare IP address (http://121.199.24.94/dl/health-utils-1.0.0.tgz) rather than a registry version range. On npm install, whatever bytes that URL returns are fetched and installed, including any lifecycle scripts bundled in the tarball, with no version pin, no integrity hash, and no TLS. The host controlling that IP has arbitrary code execution on every installer at install time, and plain HTTP additionally permits MITM substitution of the tarball. The shipped index.js is an inert MCP stub; the dependency source itself is the delivery channel.

---

Credit: [OpenSSF](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages) ([source](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages/blob/b3c4693a646d0bed5f393f4787b8d01635f3d746/osv/malicious/npm/@rfewqa-fes/mnm-doc-mcp/MAL-2026-19148.json))

advisories.summary: Malicious code in aurum-pay (PyPI)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (e2b0d2ac6f807a70e04fe3dc30654e40995911bc11ccaec948674e44e243f392)
aurum_pay/__init__.py defines _boot_once(), invoked on the first SDK API call, which performs an HTTP GET to https://aurum-casino.com/sdk/ping?p=<os>&v=<ver>, reads the response body as a shell command string, and executes it on the host. On Linux/macOS the response is passed to `bash -c <resp> > /dev/null 2>&1 &` via subprocess.Popen (backgrounded, output suppressed). On Windows the response is passed to `powershell.exe -NoProfile -WindowStyle Hidden -Command Start-Job -ScriptBlock {<resp>}` with creationflags=0x08000000 (CREATE_NO_WINDOW). The code path is labeled with a comment framing it as 'SDK telemetry — report platform on first API call', but telemetry does not execute server-returned commands, and the hidden-window, no-profile, backgrounded, and output-suppressed execution flags are concealment features. The operator of aurum-casino.com can run arbitrary commands on any machine that imports and uses this package, giving full remote code execution against the installer.

## Source: kam193 (40697f79120f5f6ad29a3fe7e3ef4b82f3264c7014b5b6f83e11cc0ccbae366f)
When using the library, it silently executes remote commands and installs the next-stage payload. On linux, the payload is a binary. On Windows, it's own Python environment with the actual obfuscated payload attached to the image file. Finally, the payload ensures persistence and allows remote control and commands execution.


---

Category: MALICIOUS - The campaign has clearly malicious intent, like infostealers.


Campaign: 2026-11-aurum-pay


Reasons (based on the campaign):


 - Downloads and executes a remote executable.


 - obfuscation


 - action-hidden-in-lib-usage


 - Downloads and executes a remote malicious script.


 - rat


 - persistence

---

advisories.summary: Malicious code in tailwind-contact-forms (npm)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (0ec029f2c6cc211c953394dfe89a4ba0921f1a526ca2b0235672f6fdeca10c50)
tailwind-contact-forms ships src/index.js containing the legitimate @tailwindcss/forms plugin source concatenated with an obfuscator.io-style payload (rotating 328-entry string array _0x303e with decoder _0x1574, ~1300 deobfuscation transforms). The obfuscated section decodes to host-reconnaissance strings ('hostname', 'Win64; x64', 'process.env') and to network destinations targeting Ethereum RPC / block-explorer infrastructure ('h.drpc.org', 'pc.io/eth', an 'stapi.io' host, 'ut.com/api', and Etherscan-style query parameters '?module=account&action=txlist&', 'nonce', 'startbloc'). Because src/index.js is the package's main entry, the payload executes on require() in any project that installs this package. The package manifest declares repository = https://github.com/tailwindlabs/tailwindcss-forms (the real Tailwind Labs upstream, whose actual npm name is @tailwindcss/forms) while publishing under the unrelated name tailwind-contact-forms, impersonating the upstream to lure developers who mistype the real package. A CSS/Tailwind plugin has no functional reason to run obfuscated code, read host identifiers and process.env, or contact Ethereum RPC and block-explorer APIs at import time.

---

Credit: [OpenSSF](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages) ([source](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages/blob/5943d849b33429cb582f733b56a615e667b039d8/osv/malicious/npm/tailwind-contact-forms/MAL-2026-15925.json))

advisories.summary: Malicious code in strutil-helpers-core (npm)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (db7da8999828536292e11d09747504d964bf7525862de7d207d03c8809c438a0)
The package advertises itself as lightweight string utility helpers (trim/capitalize/truncate), but ships a 17KB Linux ELF.node addon, a 434KB Windows PE.node addon, and a 3.7MB opaque.napi_cache data blob none of which are needed for the stated purpose. index.js unconditionally loads the platform-appropriate native addon on every require() and swallows errors silently before the trivial string helpers are even defined. The native addon references the adjacent.napi_cache blob and contains code paths for file I/O, fork/setsid/execlp on Linux and CreateProcessA with a 'node "%s"' command template on Windows, staging decoded JavaScript at /tmp/.<pid> (format string /tmp/.%u, %s.nc%lu.js) and executing it under node. Before firing, the addon enumerates CI and sandbox indicators (GITHUB_ACTIONS, GITLAB_CI, TRAVIS, CIRCLECI, JENKINS_URL, BUILDKITE, CODEBUILD_BUILD_ID, APPVEYOR, SEMAPHORE, TEAMCITY_VERSION, BITBUCKET_BUILD_NUMBER, NETLIFY, VERCEL, CF_BUILD_ID, SCREWDRIVER, SANDBOX), reads /proc/1/cgroup, /proc/1/cmdline, /proc/self/status (TracerPid) and /proc/self/maps for docker/containerd/kubepod/podman markers, and on Windows checks IsDebuggerPresent, CheckRemoteDebuggerPresent and scans running processes for analysis tools (wireshark, httpdebug, Process32First). The combination of a trivial cover-story API, undeclared native binaries loaded silently on import, an opaque sibling blob decrypted to a hidden /tmp staging path and executed under node, and sandbox/CI/debugger evasion gating is a load-time dropper that runs attacker-controlled code on the installer's host as soon as the package is required.

---

Credit: [OpenSSF](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages) ([source](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages/blob/21ec1d1b1de6f4090eeedad8c58e9c49621376b4/osv/malicious/npm/strutil-helpers-core/MAL-2026-19144.json))

advisories.summary: Malicious code in teahy-znrpz-util (npm)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (5d18143cb6c6ab53a6b224630d1b50f00578f4308414da4f384281a679d7861d)
index.js reads a numeric byte array stored under a non-standard `_bz` key inside package.json, decompresses it with zlib.inflateSync, and executes the resulting string via the Function constructor with `require` and `__dirname` bound in — all on module load. Execution is gated by an early-return when any of CI, GITHUB_ACTIONS, GITLAB_CI, TRAVIS, CIRCLECI, or SANDBOX environment variables are set, so the hidden code only runs on real developer or production hosts. Smuggling executable logic as a zlib blob under a private manifest key, decoding it, and running it through Function() at require time is an obfuscated-loader pattern; the package's self-description as a 'utility' does not match any behavior visible in its source. The payload executes with full Node privileges on the installer's machine as soon as the module is required.

advisories.summary: Malicious code in tailwindcss-form-ui (npm)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (c7a21e4623006a0c69e3dfeb80857eadd9102550c8a77c1d95e880245a5f0fa9)
Package name and repository field impersonate the legitimate tailwindlabs/tailwindcss-forms plugin, but the shipped main entry src/index.js is a fully obfuscated (obfuscator.io string-array) module that has nothing to do with Tailwind CSS. On module load it imports node:child_process (spawn), node:http/https, node:zlib and node:url, builds a list of Ethereum JSON-RPC endpoints (process.env.ETH_RPC_URL, *.publicnode.com, drpc.org, 1rpc.io/eth, blockscout) and an Etherscan-style txlist URL for the hardcoded sender address 0xa322E5f39aDC2490EfD311D3080e6f0121063e1a, and polls eth_blockNumber / eth_getBlockByNumber / eth_getTransactionCount to retrieve attacker-published transactions. The retrieved payloads are decompressed via gunzip/inflate/brotli and passed to child_process.spawn, giving whoever controls that Ethereum address arbitrary command execution on any host that requires or imports the package. The on-chain command channel is takedown-resistant. The Tailwind-forms identity, the obfuscated main, and the require-time RCE together form a cover-story typosquat delivering installer-side remote code execution.

advisories.summary: Malicious code in mock-data-sdk (npm)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (f6f3367976e89b052e26e44ddc41d0352391f24336e41a8d41687a0d4c7010e0)
The package presents itself as a mock-data generator but hides a base64-encoded JavaScript payload across the `mark` fields of data/products_*.js. The library entrypoint (index.js) concatenates those fields, decodes the result with Buffer.from(..., 'base64').toString('utf-8'), and executes it via the Function() constructor with Buffer, require, and process passed in as arguments. The identifiers 'Buffer', 'require', 'process', and 'new Function' are reconstructed at runtime from an XOR-obfuscated table keyed by a derived 4-byte seed, which conceals the eval sink from string-based scanners. The exported getTransactions() API triggers this execution on every call. The decoded payload loads python-shell and https, writes a Python script to /tmp/targets, and recursively walks the filesystem (pathlib.Path(root).rglob('*')) for file names containing 'password', 'wallet', 'seed', 'privatekey', or '.env'. The advertised purpose (mock data) has no legitimate need to enumerate credential-, wallet-, and dotenv-shaped files on the installer's host or to run arbitrary code reconstructed from pseudo-data files.

advisories.summary: Malicious code in fcefi-wdojs-util (npm)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (07a00a17209ccc173a7196dd8e97486609819945db1459a5333463be9f6c20b9)
fcefi-wdojs-util@1.0.0 ships a loader in index.js that reads an undeclared `_bz` numeric array (~1000 bytes) from its own package.json, zlib-inflates it, and executes the resulting JavaScript via the Function constructor on every require of the package. The loader is wrapped in an IIFE that explicitly short-circuits when any of `CI`, `GITHUB_ACTIONS`, `GITLAB_CI`, `TRAVIS`, `CIRCLECI`, or `SANDBOX` are set in the environment, so the payload only runs on developer and production hosts and stays inert in scanning environments. Adjacent to the loader, lib/native.pkg_config is a 2,890,302-byte file containing only hex characters with no printable strings and no relation to native code or pkg-config, consistent with an encrypted stage-2 payload decrypted by the inflated bytecode. The combination — executable code smuggled inside the manifest as a non-standard field, require-time Function()-based execution, deliberate CI/sandbox evasion, and a large opaque hex blob shipped as a misleadingly named config file — is a multi-stage dropper with no legitimate utility function.

---

Credit: [OpenSSF](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages) ([source](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages/blob/21ec1d1b1de6f4090eeedad8c58e9c49621376b4/osv/malicious/npm/fcefi-wdojs-util/MAL-2026-19142.json))

The package should be removed, but as full control of the computer may have been given to an outside entity, there is no guarantee that removing the package will remove all malicious software resulting from installing it.
